This work provides an overview of these developments, including various approaches to determining partner connections and their associated costs, as well as different optimization techniques, which are applied to a case study involving real-world data.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement.

This article proposes a single-antenna, single-frequency counterpart to our earlier research on wideband waveforming, titled "Narrowband waveforming for integrated data and energy transmission". It also presents a multi-antenna, single-frequency counterpart, referred to as "Multi-antenna waveforming for integrated data and energy transmission".

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used for studying natural language inference have limitations when expressing certain arguments with an independent meaning. Our new unary connectives draw from the Zurich Formal Grammar approach and successfully handle these situations within a categorical framework, using the means-ends calculus. These additional operators enable the expression of contextual dependencies, allowing us to provide a formal language system that comprehensively captures the examples analyzed by the Zurich Group. Our system showcases the connectives' expressive capabilities through a range of derivations, while the associated categorial interpretation method, inspired by the Zurich approach, leverages the Bruguen analysis to assign meanings to the new operators. This resulting system demonstrates the most sophisticated application yet of the means-ends analysis in a natural language framework.

In recent years, the integration of machine learning models into settings of competition has led to a growing need to address two critical issues: ensuring that the models are inherently understandable and that they can be optimized efficiently. While numerous research papers have explored both of these topics individually, our work delves into unexplored territory by simultaneously considering multiple equilibrium concepts in multiagent contexts. We establish a new metric for measuring the comprehensibility of equilibria and utilize a representative dataset to demonstrate its effectiveness. Through various multiagent scenarios, including applications involving substantial datasets, we showcase the advantages of our approach over traditional methods. Our results indicate that incorporating comprehensibility into optimization objectives leads to more reliable and understandable equilibrium solutions.

An agent-based epidemic model that spreads a virus on an evolving random graph is examined in this study. Agents connect to each other and switch connections if they contract an infection. The model is analyzed on various underlying structures as the number of connections per agent increases, and a key threshold is identified and characterized in detail. The results show that an epidemic cannot persist if agents switch connections quickly enough, but it can spread rapidly among closely connected agents if they rewire slowly enough. The model also reveals that an epidemic can occur on a random graph even if the model's parameters are set to prevent infection on a correlated graph. The findings are validated through numerical simulations on various underlying structures.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is proposed for fitting data to stochastic processes, specifically for determining probability density functions (PDFs). This framework is the foundation for a suite of tools developed to handle diverse nuclear and particle physics data sets, including those for neutrino and electro-weak parameters, parton distribution functions, and effective field theory operators. These tools provide essential functionality for working with complex datasets, such as reweighting, metropolis-weighted averages, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples, and are the key components of the popular xqcd fit package.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple state dimensions, reinforcement learning agents often employ experience replay to re-use previously collected, rich data. Standard experience replay utilizes a fixed sampling method, drawing unique observations randomly from the memory buffer. These observations are then used to compute a single representative target value for each episode. We introduce an adaptive approach to reduce target value variance by selecting samples that are closely related to the current policy. This is achieved by sampling pairs of transitions that have experienced high returns under the current policy. As a result, our proposed algorithm exhibits improved performance compared to state-of-the-art policy optimization methods on challenging tasks, including Hopper and Walker2d from the Gymathlon.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library that makes it easy to work with polynomial operators used in the quantum many-body theory by creating a specialized dialect for exact diagonalization. This library provides an efficient and straightforward way for developers to define complex quantum models, perform calculations of matrix elements, and initialize objects for numerical simulations. Furthermore, it serves as a powerful problem-solving framework that can tackle various computational tasks encountered in the field.

We utilized full-potential lattice dynamics to determine the electronic structure and superconducting gap structure of the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ superconductor. Our method directly computes the quasiparticle interaction with the crystal lattice, bypassing any assumptions regarding the feasibility of the linear response theory. Through this approach, we derived the superconducting gap structure and obtained the superconducting energy gap values at various momenta, which show an energy difference of approximately 2$MeV$ between the center and the edge of the full Brillouin zone. Our results also indicate that the superconducting gap structure changes from the $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave type to the $d+f$-wave type with increasing energy. Furthermore, we found that the superconducting gap structure exhibits $C_4$ symmetry breaking, and that the zero-line gaps appear at the edge of the full Brillouin zone with increasing energy. Our study is in line with the recent experimental findings of anomalous magnetic relaxation and edge-centered superconducting gap structures.

Recently, two new equations were proposed, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation, which both effectively convert a quadratic operator in a specific variable into a squared form. A comparison shows that the superbosonization equation is more versatile and can be applied across multiple domains, whereas the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is specifically tailored for matrix quadratic equations.

The study reports on measuring top quark polarization in t-channel single top quark production using 8 TeV pp collision data, totaling 19.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity, collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC. The measurement is based on the observation of the decay to certain final states with a lepton and without a lepton. For leptonic decays, a fit to certain angular distributions identified with s-channel contribution determined the polarization value, yielding -0.004 ± 0.013 (statistic) ± 0.015 (systematic) or -0.04 ± 0.013. For non-lepton decays, a similar approach yielded a polarization value of 0.056 ± 0.014 (statistic) ± 0.014 (systematic) or 0.05 ± 0.014. The measurement exceeds previous limits and is consistent with top quark helicity conservation.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the magnetic properties of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our results reveal that the spin-lattice relaxation mechanism transitions from an initial antiferromagnetic arrangement to a more complex, orthogonally rotated state as the number of layers increases beyond ten. Notably, this rotational transition persists even in the absence of long-range magnetic order, suggesting a more intricate relationship between magnetism and structural distortion in these materials.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions.

Our research offers a mathematical analysis and maximum throughput calculation for a complex wireless communication system, utilizing reflective surfaces and multiple antennas while considering factors like correlated signal transmission and a common transmission power limitation. By developing a new approach to determine the ergodic throughput, we also address various performance metrics, including the distribution of a key system performance metric and a throughput comparison between two different system configurations. Furthermore, our findings are verified using numerical simulations and a specialized hardware system.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a cutting-edge tool for conducting comprehensive N-body simulations quickly, while maintaining precise predictions in line with various modified gravity models, specifically those that alter the gravitational force in a scale-dependent manner. This innovative method leverages the original GLEAM code and employs an efficient approach to address potential collisions in N-body systems. For a class of modified gravity models known as conformal coupling models, we discovered that small-scale discrepancies can be significant, thus requiring a more sophisticated treatment. Nonetheless, MG-GLAM delivers reliable results comparable to state-of-the-art N-body simulations for a substantial portion of these models, at a fraction of the computational cost.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension of the popular MediaWiki platform, designed to support collaborative research through high-quality data visualization tools and a user-friendly interface. Originally developed to support the analysis of complex systems data, WorkingWiki enables users to easily create interactive dashboards, stream real-time data, and facilitate collaborative work via asynchronous discussions and task management. With its intuitive syntax for creating interactive dashboards based on R programming language functions, users can seamlessly integrate external tools and services, while maintaining the security and reliability that underpins the MediaWiki infrastructure. Furthermore, WorkingWiki is poised to revolutionize the way research teams work together, promote transparency in research processes, and make information more accessible through dynamic, easily shareable dashboards.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame in a crossflow, while acoustically forced with a premixed flame model that responds actively to temperature fluctuations. To achieve this, the model utilizes an intrinsic basis function method to define the flame's dynamics, resulting in a reduced-dimensionality representation that can account for oscillatory phenomena. The model is then expanded into a linearized form in terms of small disturbances, and this form is validated through comparison with comprehensive nonlinear simulations for various acoustic excitation levels. The findings indicate that the model accurately captures the oscillatory behavior of the flame when driven by transverse modes, and that it can provide insight into the mechanisms underlying combustion instability. However, the model's performance declines in cases involving longitudinal modes and channeled flows, where non-linear effects play a more significant role.

Recent discoveries in topological physics, such as the topological insulators, have shed light on a long-forgetten aspect of Hall conductivity in the solar spectrum. This project's goal is to investigate topological properties in solar oscillations, which involve examining the continuum spectrum of stellar adiabatic oscillations for signs of a non-zero Berry curvature and flux through the entire solar frequency space. By using a new numerical approach, this study calculates the Berry curvature and flux for both plane-wave and non-plane-wave modes, and maps the spectral properties of solar oscillations in a four-dimensional space, comprising frequency, wavelength, polarization, and spatial pattern. The results indicate that solar oscillations exhibit high Chern numbers, representing multiple topological insulating phases within the stellar Hall conductivity spectrum. Furthermore, by relating the solar Hall conductivity to magnetized power dissipation, this study finds a distinct magnetized power distribution pattern, which could potentially be used as an indicator for detecting topological states in stars.

We present a novel, flexible approach for determining the existence of travelling chimeras and synchronized clusters in networks of coupled oscillators. Our method is unbounded and unhindered by the restrictions associated with the previously established conditions, allowing us to investigate a wide range of network configurations. We subsequently apply this method to examine the dynamics of three distinct types of network architectures, consisting of coupled ring networks featuring multiple clusters, as well as networks representing a range of geographical configurations, including islands and a circular array. Our analysis reveals a wide range of functional patterns, including travelling chimeras, clustered synchronizations, and patterns involving multiple clusters. Notably, our findings show that the precision of our method is comparable to that of previously established techniques when applied to a previously studied ring network.

In two-dimensional lattice gases where interactions occur between non-adjacent sites, 
we observe a unique shift in decay rates within the semi-Fock representation, 
especially in a two-site interaction model on a square lattice. 
This result triggers a finite-density phase and separates high-density clusters from isolated sites. 
A similar multi-site interaction model on a triangular lattice also exhibits this phenomenon. 
However, in both cases, the semi-Fock representation fails to capture the isolated site phase. 
In the two-site interaction model, the semi-Fock representation yields an exact solution using the spin-1/2 representation, 
while in the multi-site interaction model, it yields an approximate solution using the Gershkowitch scheme. 
Both solutions reveal the emergence of a decay rate zero mode within the semi-Fock representation. 
The associated correlation function behaves like that of an free fermion or spin-1/2 system, 
while the semi-Fock representation fails to capture the isolated site phase due to a zero-mode instability. 
In the two-site interaction model, the exact solution confirms the emergence of a finite-density cluster phase. 
In the multi-site interaction model, the approximate solution confirms the emergence of a decay rate zero mode and the cluster phase. 
Both models exhibit a cluster phase with distinct decay rates within and outside this region. 
The associated correlation function displays an exponential increase followed by a linear increase in the cluster region. 
The cluster region is characterized by rapid decay within this

We investigate how neutrinos interact with ultralight scalar dark matter, considering the impact on zero-neutrino double beta decay, which could occur if a primordial density perturbation caused a slight over-density of neutrinos in certain regions of space. As a result, we might observe an unusually high rate of zero-neutrino double beta decay in a specific location. Our analysis includes the effects of both neutrino interactions with the dark matter and neutrino self-interactions, and we establish the conditions under which these interactions could lead to an exceptionally high rate of zero-neutrino double beta decay. We also examine the constraints imposed by observational data regarding the density fluctuations in the early universe and find that they limit the possibility of significantly increasing the rate of zero-neutrino double beta decay through the actions of ultralight dark matter.

The observations of extremely energetic photons coming from the solar direction pose a mystery. To tackle this, a statistical model is developed to account for photons above an incredibly high energy threshold. It is based on a comprehensive understanding of the solar magnetic field's behavior and considers the scalar and tensor components of photons interacting with solars magnetic field. The model takes into consideration the implications of Cerenkov radiation on photons and accounts for photons that result from this process, as well as those produced when magnetic field fluctuations cause photons to become undetectable, thus fitting with data from the Fermi-Gamma Ray Observatory.

Nonlocal gravity theory is examined in this work to determine its underlying framework and the constitutive relationships that govern it. The nonlocal theory is shown to be based on a specific infinite-order differential operator, $\Delta^\infty$, associated with the Hadamard feature. This results in a modified Poisson equation that can be expressed in terms of $\Delta^\infty$ applied to the conventional gravitational potential. The constitutive relationship for nonlocal gravity is then derived from a comprehensive nonlocal continuity equation, yielding an explicit formula involving $\Delta^\infty$ applied to the conventional gravitational field. The infinite-order differential operator $\Delta^\infty$ is represented in terms of conventional differential operators, and its applications are explored. Furthermore, a finite-order approximation of the nonlocal gravity theory is derived and shown to align with existing models.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing these conflicts is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Structure (CRDS) approach. Despite existing implementations, building and optimizing CRDS for different use cases and systems is difficult due to the lack of a clear design methodology. To address this gap, the proposed Remove-Win framework provides a design solution for building efficient CRDS. Initially, the framework is applied to develop a new variant of the Golang implementation of the Multiversion Counting Quorum (MV-CQ) data type. The resulting MV-CQ-R implementation outperforms the existing MV-CQ-G by achieving a 40% boost in write performance and a 30% improvement in read performance. The study also validates the effectiveness of the Remove-Win framework by analyzing the challenges faced in designing MV-CQ-R and the benefits derived from the approach.

To further understand the underlying biology of complex traits influenced by numerous genetic factors, we introduced a multi-factorial approach using genomic data from multiple sources. This approach involves two main components: 1) incorporating functional genomic data to identify active genes across various tissues and life stages, and 2) combining genome-wide association studies to map genetic variants associated with specific traits. We applied this approach to 18 human traits and conducted a comprehensive analysis of genetic variants, mapping them to specific positions in the genome and associating them with traits through linkage to protein-coding genes. Our results show that most protein-coding genes are active across multiple stages of life and tissues, but only a small fraction of them are linked to specific traits and are active in relevant tissues at relevant life stages. Furthermore, active genes in a particular trait are often found in different tissues, and many of these genes are involved in a range of cellular processes, including DNA repair, protein modification, transport, and RNA processing. Additionally, we identified several key regulatory elements influencing expression of genes associated with specific traits and involved in various stages of gene expression, including transcription, splicing, and translation. Our study provides new insights into the complex interplay of genetic and functional elements that contribute to the variability of 18 important human traits.

This paper discusses the capabilities of the Large Hadron Collider to investigate subatomic substructures in matter by examining di-photon events produced when protons collide at extremely high energies. To do this, the researchers re-examined existing data from the LHC's operation within its designated safety margins, known as the "5 TeV contour". They then considered what insights might be gained from future collisions at full power, as well as how the signal-to-noise ratio of substructure searches might be improved through more precise measurements of the internal workings of protons. Additionally, they explored ways to differentiate between the effects of substructures and other influences that could also contribute to larger-than-expected particle sizes.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low mass loss rates go into dormancy for longer periods. This study delves into the timing of outbursts in neutron star binaries and contrasts it with the lack of activity in the Galactic Centre's quiescent X-ray binaries to provide supporting evidence for the majority of these latter sources being neutron star binaries. By examining the published data of all known neutron star binaries that have outbursted at least twice, this study determines the median recurrence interval of these systems to be roughly 1.5 years. Furthermore, by applying statistical techniques and eliminating systems with extremely short or long recurrence intervals, it is found that the majority of the Galactic Centre's quiescent X-ray binaries have similar characteristics to the broader population of neutron star binaries, with a median recurrence interval of approximately 2.5 years.

The number of wide binary stars in various populations can be employed as a means of experimenting with the principles of gravity. Consequently, multiple studies have undertaken this test, yielding results that either support gravity's standard form or an alternative theory. Nonetheless, existing research on this topic remains inconclusive due to methodological issues in estimating binary star populations. In our study, we extracted a comprehensive sample of 1,000,000 binary stars drawn from a realistic population of 2 million stars, generated using the BinClus program. Our analysis involved comparing observed and predicted wide binary population distributions across various parameters, including magnitude, mass, metal content, and spin. The most influential factor in population synthesis was the choice of equation of state used in such models. Therefore, in order to make an unbiased test of gravity, it is essential to select wide binary stars that are resistant to formation influences and are thus less biased. Our findings also indicate that wide binary stars offering the greatest insight into the nature of gravity are composed of low-mass stars with moderate metal content, found in significant numbers in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.

We analyzed a massive radio source catalog, examining the properties of radio sources with specific characteristics, including orientation indicators and environment features, in relation to their angular size. Our study utilized a large radio source sample from the Faint Radio Survey, involving over 10,000 sources, and employed statistical techniques called stacking. By stacking images of radio sources with particular features, we gathered information about their average properties. Our main findings showed that radio sources with larger angular sizes tend to have lower brightness values, are more strongly linked to galaxy clusters, and have greater projected distances from these clusters. They also tend to be associated with cooler molecular gas and have different gas phases than smaller sources. Our study indicates that radio sources with larger angular sizes represent a separate subgroup than smaller sources, with distinct physical properties and environmental relationships.

We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional shocks in stellar explosions, specifically fast forward shocks and reverse shocks, using numerical simulations. The waves cause the shock to become unstable and break up, finally dissipating its energy through envelope heating. The heating rate of the envelope is found to be directly proportional to the square of the amplitude of the wave and varies inversely with the third power of the wavelength. The proportionality constant is determined through simulations of SDOK-like explosions. The presence of waves is shown to increase the energy released by the shock by up to two orders of magnitude over a period of several days following the explosion, with the effect depending on the grain size. The presence of waves also alters the distribution of energy in the envelope, with a greater proportion being directed towards higher frequencies. The impact of waves on the evolution of the shock and envelope are found to vary with mass loss rate, with the highest rates resulting in the strongest shocks and most rapid cooling. The potential for waves to contribute to the formation of supernovae-like explosions is also explored.

This brief investigation seeks to explain the concept of geometric modularity recently introduced by Diamond, Hansen, and Yun. We discuss an alternate approach using the geometric Ring Class Field theory of Buzzard, Kelsey, and Yun. This approach provides a clear, self-contained proof of the conjecture in Yun's paper, specifically the non-triviality of the geometric Selmer group for weight 2, level 1, Serre weights. We also discuss an algebraic analog of geometric modularity and its implications. Additionally, we examine potential connections between geometric modularity and the Weighted Serre's Conjecture.

Momentum-conserving electron and spin scattering events, often overlooked in average approaches, are scrutinized in this study for their impact on nonequilibrium dynamics in materials. A combination of analytical and numerical methods is used to demonstrate the critical role these events play in spawning both electron and spin modes that are coupled with vibrations in solids, as well as the creation of new phonon states that are charged with electrical current and magnetization. These findings are also illustrated through a series of nonequilibrium laser-based experiments designed to manipulate electron spin.

Precise knowledge of a module's structure is not always necessary to determine its distribution into basic submodules, and this knowledge does not necessarily provide a full understanding of the module's distribution. By examining the relationship between a module and its submodules, specifically through the $\tau$-tilting module's representation, we can determine this distribution. Furthermore, by establishing the connection between a module's representation and that of its submodules, we can infer additional information about the module's structure. In this talk, we will explore how the $\tau$-tilting module's representation can be used to identify a module's distribution into basic submodules.

Recent advances in neural networks for conversational dialogue have largely been made by applying pre-trained models and Sequence-to-Sequence techniques, yet they fall short when compared to human performance in controlled dialogue tasks. One key reason for this lag is the failure to account for semantic variety within a dialogue's vocabulary, a shortcoming exacerbated by the limited lexical overlap typically found between dialogue utterances. To address this issue, we introduce the SemAntic Dialogue Dataset, which incorporates the Natural Language Inference Framework to capture the inherent polysemy present in a dialogue's vocabulary. This dataset enables the simultaneous improvement of both semantic representation and dialogue generation capabilities. In our research, we selected the Universal Sentence Encoder as our baseline multi-task learner and achieved promising results by demonstrating a 9% boost in semantic accuracy and a 23% gain in dialogue task performance when compared to a single-task approach.

Automated driving systems depend on predictive modules to assess risks and avoid accidents, however, their current implementation is hindered by expensive and complex technologies. A novel approach has been developed for classifying high-risk situations from a dataset of lane change video clips using deep learning techniques. The proposed system combines a spatiotemporal neural network with a facial recognition algorithm to recognize and map key point movements over time. The performance of this system was compared to several benchmark models, revealing its highest accuracy rate of 96.1% in predicting high-risk situations.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a challenge in quantifying the impact of experimental factors 
such as background levels, feed-through from other decays, and particle reconstruction efficiencies 
which can complicate the interpretation of results. This study aims to address these difficulties 
by presenting a mathematical framework that accounts for these experimental limitations. A key aspect 
of this framework is the derivation of formulas to calculate key metrics including efficiency, 
background level, and feed-through amplitude parameters. Additionally, this study proposes strategies 
for determining key parameters entering the amplitude analysis formulation. Notably, this formulation 
can be expressed in a way that quantifies the influence of experimental factors on observed distributions 
without referring to the original decay process. Consequently, this study offers methods for comparing 
different experimental measurements, combining results from amplitude analyses across different studies, 
and interpreting findings in presence of significant background levels.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach is presented that directly targets the challenging cases, using a parameterized approach capable of efficiently handling instances where the number of edge crossings exceeds a specified threshold. This new approach builds on previous work utilizing vertex splitting as a strategy to minimize crossings, and refines the technique to utilize a more manageable parameter in its algorithm. The properties of this refined approach are examined, and it is demonstrated that it resolves a fundamental problem with the earlier splitting method. Furthermore, this new approach is effectively integrated with existing methods for ranking vertices and adjusting the layout.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, nonetheless, their limited ability to adapt to new data efficiently and systematically presents a significant challenge. The field of incremental learning addresses this issue by developing techniques that enable networks to incorporate fresh training data without necessity for prior knowledge. Although substantial progress has been made, the field still faces crucial hurdles due to ongoing changes in data distributions and class formations. This paper introduces two novel approaches to tackle two crucial problems in incremental learning: data distribution shifts and class formation changes. It also compares the effectiveness of these approaches in relation to existing techniques through comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing the significant performance improvements achieved.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking with thrusters. We have developed a variable-footplant pattern that maintains balance and efficiency. To operate within desired bounds, we have implemented an algorithm to regulate speed, foot angle, and pressure. To handle unexpected events, we have also designed a stabilization system using thrusters. We will demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by testing the strategy on a simulated and physical bipedal robot.

We define a new classification of valued domains through a comprehensive residue map, which we call "total" for being a combination of all partial residue maps. Our key observation is that this classification is equivalent to a domains' classification based on their associated total valuation chain. Notably, one-way chains, in particular, parallel chains, play a crucial role in this context, mirroring the role of linear chains in the classification of valued fields. Additionally, we demonstrate that domains with a total residue map can also be classified using their Krull dimension, which is one higher than the dimension of their residue field.

In order to mitigate the negative effects of trace caching on energy efficiency, this work introduces a novel technique called HyperDegrade. By selectively discarding precise address information from cache tags, HyperDegrade aims to take advantage of the characteristics of real workloads to deliver significant improvements in energy performance. Experiments conducted on actual applications and benchmarks have shown that HyperDegrade can lead to a notable decrease in energy consumption, ranging from 8 to 24%, without causing a noticeable slowdown in performance. Furthermore, HyperDegrade's benefits in energy performance are found to be independent of cache size. To further explore the potential of HyperDegrade, this study also examines various degradation strategies, proposes an efficient design for the technique, and provides insights into the factors that influence energy performance in modern systems.

We investigate whether new Higgs interactions, beyond the Standard Model, can resolve the discrepancy in the hadronic part of the muon g-2. To this end, we develop a comprehensive analysis of all possible new Higgs contributions, considering both effective field theory operators and direct interactions through new heavy physics. Employing a dimensionless effective potential for the Higgs field, we derive a precise expression for the muon electric dipole operator. We then proceed to examine specific scenarios for new physics scales and spurion couplings. Through a thorough scan of parameter space, we clarify the regions that could resolve the g-2 anomaly. We further establish the distinct signatures that such scenarios would imprint on Higgs physics, such as anomalous forward backward asymmetries or non-standard high-energy diphoton spectra. Moreover, we explore the implications of these solutions for other low-energy phenomena like lepton flavor non-universality (LFUV) and CP violation in neutral mesons.

A novel approach is presented for determining the hadronic decay sequence in charm hadron decays, utilizing data from the Belle experiment. By analyzing events featuring a muon and an electron, researchers can identify pairs of decay products that are correlated in energy and direction. This allows for the creation of events featuring a specific sequence of hadronic decays, thereby determining the decay sequence based on measured quantities. It is shown that this method is an effective way to identify decay sequences, even when doing so generally. Furthermore, with a large data set, the angle between the electron and the antineutrino's direction can be measured, providing a means to determine the CP-violating phase, γ, through interference in decay paths. This method is a valuable tool for studying the CP-violating phase in hadron decays.

We define a new reordering operation for n-digit Newton polygons, which we call the "hierarchy operation." This new operation mirrors the properties of the Permutahedron, specifically inheriting patterns seen in the extended flag variety. We then demonstrate that the hierarchy operation is compatible with the "sum" operation of Newton polygons, effectively allowing the creation of a rich set of relations among these polygons. These preorders are relevant to the study of classical and welded links via their Kauffman bracket skein module, as they provide a way to encode and study these links in a higher-dimensional space.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-string version of the Fox-Hatcher map with the Gramain's 2-string version yields a invariant for links, specifically a 3rd-order Vassiliev invariant. This combination result arises from modifying the Gramain's map so that its input involves a 3-fold covering of the link's complement, in turn producing a relation with the Fox-Hatcher map after accounting for the Milnor's Moore context. Furthermore, we employ this modified Gramain's map to create an explicit expression for an invariant of order three, thereby answering a previous question posed by the Vassiliev archive.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are limited to less than 0.8 eV/c^2. In this study, we analyze how combining this upper limit with an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, around 0.4 eV/c^2 as indicated by stellar stability, may lead to the complete restriction of available parameter space for neutrino masses in the coming years. This research is then expanded to consider sterile neutrinos, establishing a minimum mass for a single such neutrino flavour.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices.

In this research, we examine how a group of autonomous agents, capable of performing computational tasks while being influenced by external factors, coordinate their actions when connected in a network. We establish conditions under which these agents can coordinate their actions through a routine of observation, computation, and communication. We also investigate the impact of changing the structure of their network on the effectiveness of their coordination. Finally, we show that by following a specific approach, agents can determine the optimal method for coordinating their actions. This research has the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient cyber physical systems.

As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity.

As federated learning progresses, many applications now utilize vertical FL to effectively combine the resources of multiple participants while minimizing data transfer. However, combining data in this manner poses a more complex privacy challenge. Our research reveals that lightweight anti-privacy attacks are both feasible and crucial in a FL setting, especially when dealing with sensitive medical data. We present a method using ensemble techniques to enhance the accuracy of models trained with privacy attacks, and our experimental results show that this method yields significant improvements over existing approaches. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of securely transmitting encrypted model updates and suggests using post-processing techniques to improve the efficiency of encryption methods.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their use is limited by the computationally intensive nature of pairwise evaluations between data points. To overcome this, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, making them a popular choice for kernel-based methods. Although widely adopted, this approach has a significant drawback, as it relies on the assumption that the kernel function is constant across the Fourier features, which can lead to subpar performance when data is scarce. In response to this limitation, this study presents an alternative method for estimating kernels that leverages a more sophisticated approach tailored to specific types of kernels, resulting in consistently superior outcomes, particularly in scenarios where data sets are limited.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the wreath product's equivalent form. Furthermore, we found that this incorporation can be divided into manageable parts, or components, known as semirecurrent and prediagonal subgroups, which together synthesize the original group's structure. Our findings also reveal that the subgroups responsible for the combined, or product action are distinct from those responsible for the individual actions. We applied this understanding to a specific instance, the symmetric group S_n, and derived its representation under combined action, thereby solving an unresolved problem. Our solution breaks down complex combined actions into more accessible, simpler actions, and demonstrates a link between combined actions and a specific pattern in group tables, or Cayley tables.

This research paper examines how Mobius transformations affect the scalar curvature of compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces in $n+2$ dimensional sphere space. We have derived a range of results indicating that certain conformally flat hypersurfaces with constant Mobius curvature are highly adaptable and can be modified through Mobius transformations to produce a wide range of values for their scalar curvature. We have also determined that certain conformally flat hypersurfaces with this property of constant Mobius curvature, when projected onto the hypersurfaces themselves, are essentially a flexibility theorem. This flexibility applies regardless of whether the hypersurfaces are endowed with a flat Euclidean metric or not.

In rare congenital heart diseases, surgical planning requires precise pre-operative evaluation. Advanced imaging techniques, specifically CMR, have become essential for this process. Although automated segmentation of abnormal heart structures poses a challenge for the generalization of models trained on normal heart data, our study investigates whether a CMR-based UNet model trained on normal heart anatomy can effectively segment abnormal heart structures before surgery. To achieve this, we compiled a dataset of 5517 2D slice images from 107 different CMR exams for both training and testing the UNet model. The results of our study showed a high level of accuracy for the model in identifying and segmenting left and right ventricles as well as the myocardium in both healthy and diseased heart cases. With a focus on accuracy rather than speed, our UNet-based solution achieved a score of 0.857 for the left ventricle, 0.878 for the right ventricle, and 0.871 for the myocardium. These findings demonstrate the potential for automatic transfer learning in difficult medical imaging cases.

This study focuses on a particular type of microstructurally motivated degradation model, specifically those that incorporate a degradation gradient in the context of small strain linear elasticity. A model that incorporates a degradation gradient has been recently proposed by Miehe and Mecklenburg, and this work aims to critically examine it. A proposed framework is then introduced to generalize the model, considering various forms of degradation and their respective effects. The generalized framework is applied to two specific scenarios: one with isotropic degradation and another with anisotropic degradation, and numerical implementations are provided for both cases. The feasibility of the proposed method is then demonstrated through numerical simulations of a degradation test and a numerical investigation of a composite material's degradation.

A new approach to efficient wireless communication is proposed in this paper, utilizing a method where information and energy are shared through a single medium. To achieve optimal performance, a multi-service wireless network has been formulated as an optimization problem subject to specific constraints. In this formulation, each user can either receive information and energy, or information only, depending on their specific requirements. To solve this problem, a method based on Lagrange multipliers has been developed, but due to the complexity of the problem, a gradient-based iterative algorithm is proposed instead. This algorithm involves each user optimizing their own resource allocation, but yields a suboptimal solution. To improve the efficiency of the algorithm, a method has been proposed where the center system can influence the users' behavior by adjusting a certain parameter. This parameter is determined by the center system, but is based on the users' individual utility functions. Simulation results have shown that the proposed algorithm can provide a close approximation to the optimal solution, and has advantages in terms of convergence speed.

Object detection in an image is often predicted using a single primary class or several classes that are assumed to be relevant, without verifying the accuracy of this assumption. However, this approach can result in both missed detections and inaccurate predictions when assuming certain objects are present. In fact, studies have shown that when no prior knowledge is used to identify relevant classes, around 40% of identified objects are considered irrelevant. To address this issue, I propose examining all visible objects in an image instead of relying on assumptions about their presence. This is achievable through a simple yet effective method that leverages segmentation and refined predictions to significantly improve accuracy. My experiments demonstrate a notable 12% enhancement in average precision when comparing the proposed approach to traditional methods.

In analyzing complex systems with multiple influencing factors, researchers often turn to conditional models for a detailed understanding. These models are particularly useful for studying how specific variables impact the system's behavior, but their own underlying mechanics may be difficult to interpret without context. To better grasp these mechanisms, a new set of mathematical tools is developed to extract implicit patterns of influence from conditional models, even if they involve continuous and nonlinear relationships. A specific application is showcased in analyzing the impact of economic indicators on voter intentions in the 2008 US presidential election, demonstrating how researchers can identify implicit interaction effects between variables and assess their statistical significance. The proposed method is versatile and can be adapted to address key questions in various fields with complex data sets.

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to tackle this problem, we must first understand the challenges posed by linguistic heterogeneity, including the diversity of word orders, availability of contextual information, and influence of prior knowledge. In this competition, we would draw upon experiences gained from participating in the 2021 Shared Task on WSD, where our team achieved notable success with limited manual interventions. To achieve this, we employed a series of automated techniques to create GlossBERT, a BERT-based model capable of generating word-specific embeddings that can differentiate between various senses of polysemous words. The code and pre-trained models are available for download at https://github.com/alextseng23/Huang-et-al-2021-SRWSD.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to master, 
as demonstrated by the success of human planners and the simplicity of fundamental 
theories like Episodic Theory (ET). Although recent machine learning models excel 
at ordering events, they behave optimally in contexts where order doesn't matter 
and fail to comprehend essential human procedural knowledge, such as understanding 
the temporal relationships indicated by verbs and the sequential structure of 
instructions. To better grasp this knowledge, we examine a set of book guides 
from Wikipedia that provide complex, diverse sequences of actions. Our analysis 
shows that these book guides exhibit a range of temporal relationships, including 
static, sequential, and concurrent scenarios, as well as recurrent patterns and 
conditional steps, all expressed through a variety of verbs and by incorporating 
external references. To examine how well the automatic sequences match the 
original guides, we created both a machine learning model and a simple rule-based 
system to sequence events on their own and compared them to the expert-planned 
events from Wikipedia. Our experiments revealed that both models struggle to 
accomplish this task, demonstrating a significant gap between human procedural 
understanding and machine learning abilities. To bridge this gap, we believe it 
is crucial to develop a robust, general-purpose model that can interpret the 
temporal aspects of verbs and learn from complex, unordered sequences of actions.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a more detailed analysis of the impact of a network attack on individual nodes within a Cayley tree network. The authors seek to identify the distribution of the sizes of impact, which they refer to as an "avalanche," and explore whether there are specific patterns or characteristics that certain nodes exhibit during an attack. This research aims to provide insights that can be used to develop more effective strategies for managing the spread of information and diseases in networks.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

Next-generation gravitational wave detectors will likely involve laser interferometry with incredible sensitivity, however, there's a significant challenge limiting their performance - noise caused by seismic vibrations. By manipulating a new design, we're exploring the potential to significantly reduce this noise using a unique "sloshing-Sagnac" design where the movement of the detector is mirrored in the laser beam. This involves creating an intricate system of moving mirrors and an etalon to control the frequency of the laser, all while maintaining the precision required for gravitational wave detection. Using existing materials, we've calculated that such a design could reduce seismic noise by a remarkable 10 times, simply by increasing the frequency of the measurement. Our research showcases that the sloshing-Sagnac design is feasible with current technology and that it offers promising avenues for further optimization.

Recent advancements in massive MIMO and millimeter wave technology have significant implications for future high-performance wireless networks.  However, both technologies pose important visibility region challenges when implementing their random access protocols.  Currently, most protocol designs assume a circular visibility region, yet actual regions are more complex and non-circular in nature.  Research has shown that the visibility regions in MIMO and millimeter wave systems can be highly variable and even intersect with neighboring users' transmission zones.  Consequently, this is causing a surge in interest for implementing protocols that take into account the actual shapes and positions of these regions.  Therefore, researchers have proposed an new XL-MIMO RAMAN protocol that takes into account the real shapes and positions of these regions.  However, the performance of this new protocol has not been thoroughly analyzed.  Therefore, we are analyzing the performance of XL-MIMO RAMAN when the visibility regions do not intersect and when they do intersect.  Our results show that the protocol's performance is highly dependent on several key factors including the number of MIMO antennas, millimeter wave frequency, and distance between users.  Furthermore, we have also derived a new closed-form expression for the throughput of XL-MIMO RAMAN when the visibility regions do not intersect.  Our findings have significant implications for the design of future high-performance wireless networks that utilize massive MIMO and millimeter wave technology.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological organization of protoplanetary disk structures is similar to that of the solar neighborhood. However, the natural occurrence of structures in protoplanetary disks needs to be explained. This work suggests that protoplanetary disks undergo a process called vertical shear instability, forming ring-like and spiral patterns as a result. In our previous study, we analyzed the stability of a laboratory model mimicking conditions in a protoplanetary environment and discovered that spiral density enhancements and vortex rings formed due to the vertical shear instability. In this study, we utilize a numerical model to simulate a range of protoplanetary disks under various conditions, observing the formation of spiral density enhancements and vortex rings in these environments. Our findings indicate that the formation of these structures can be observed in the dust continuum using current radio telescopes, such as ALMA, within a few thousands of years. The stability of protoplanetary disks is influenced by several factors, including the ratio of the viscosity of the gas to the viscosity of the solid particles, the how the solid particles are distributed, and the temperature of the gas. Our predictions, based on these factors, are compared to observations made by ALMA in a diagram, showing a possible range in which the vertical shear instability may be observed.

The 'Big Apple' strength, a parameter relating the volume part of the symmetry energy to the incompressibility coefficient of nuclear matter, is examined in this report. Various models of the energy density functional are used to determine its value, and a range of values is found to be consistent with existing nuclear data. A value of approximately -34 is estimated for the 'Big Apple' coefficient, and this is found to be necessary for maintaining the predicted stability of neutron stars.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing correlated orbitals and constructing Wannier functions in the model. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, our study shows that this assumption can lead to inaccuracies. For instance, a more complex spectral structure is revealed when the model incorporates additional correlated orbitals, a phenomenon not seen in the simpler model. Utilizing the Fork Tensor Product State impurity solver allows us to resolve high-frequency differences and obtain more precise results. Our results indicate that using this solver for full 5-band DMFT calculations yields spectral structures consistent with experiments, showcasing the solver's ability to perform such complex calculations directly on the real-frequency axis.

We have analytically proven that using multiple motional modes in Motional-Parity gates can provide frequency stability, a crucial aspect for large-scale quantum computing. To achieve this, we used a technique where some modes are prepared in a steady-state while others are conditioned on a specific state. This leads to a balanced superposition of states across all modes, creating a stable parity gate when applied at a specific frequency. We have also found that using two modes is sufficient to create a stable parity gate, which is an important finding because it overcomes a major challenge in quantum computing. We have already demonstrated the feasibility of this method experimentally using two motional modes in an ion trap, and we have even created a record number of entanglement pairs using this method.

Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that certain arrangements of atoms in cubic perovskites can resist polarization despite strong electric fields. By applying machine learning to minimize costs and simulations to find the optimal arrangements, we've discovered new polarization-resistant structures hidden within a commonly studied oxide, nickel-only terminated potassium niobate. This provides a clear foundation for understanding the unique properties of these materials and how they can be optimized for specific uses.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid-state materials hosting massless Dirac fermions, which are also closely related to the fractional quantum Hall effect in the limit of exact parity symmetry. Unfortunately, studies have consistently shown that these Dirac points are prone to instability due to strong electronic interactions. This could potentially result in novel states of matter, such as heavy chiral fermions or spinless bosons, which emerge when the Dirac points collapse and merge with a nearby charge neutrality plane. In this study, we've identified monolayer nickelate as an ideal material system where Dirac fermions naturally reside near nearby planes of high charge density. By employing a combination of first-principles calculations and a restricted electronic model, we've demonstrated that strong electronic interactions may induce a spontaneous formation of polarization in the nickelate's lattice, giving rise to a unique three-component order parameter. This parameter distinguishes between various possible states of matter that could emerge in the system and may be used to investigate the effect of driving a Dirac point into the nearby high-density plane on the resulting physics. Our calculations indicate that nickelate exhibits a complex phase diagram with intertwined effects of electron interaction, strain, and spin-orbit coupling, resulting in the stabilization of a novel quantum state: a strongly interacting Dirac metal that exhibits both chiral edge modes and superconductivity.

We present a multi-dimensional growth model that captures the dynamics of two overlapping populations experiencing exponential growth. This model can also represent ratios of different populations, such as sex ratios in various species. Our model is a systematic reduction of a stochastic process described by Cox-Ingersoll-Randall differential equations. We demonstrate the uniqueness of the positive equilibrium point and the stability of this equilibrium point through linearization. We then apply our model to analyze the dynamics of female mammals in a population of growing size, observing that the model is susceptible to phase shift chaos. Additionally, we investigate the impact of changing population density on growth rates and the resulting periodic and turbulent dynamics.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the decay of kaons into pi-zero, an electron and neutrally charged particles, they examined various mass ranges of these leptons. Combining existing data with statistical tools, they predicted NA62 could restrict the constant of interaction to a particularly narrow range, thereby testing theoretical predictions about the masses of these leptons.

In a Sagnac interferometer, light experiences two different spacetime geometries when moving in opposite directions. This uniqueness results in a phenomenon known as spectral shift anomaly, where the two light paths exhibit distinct frequencies. While this discrepancy is generally attributed to the Doppler effect, a more in-depth analysis is required in scenarios involving high-speed observers. In this analysis, we employ a tensorial approach to quantify the spectral shift anomaly and calculate the frequency difference between the two light paths. This calculation yields a key equation that showcases the complex relationship between the spectral shift anomaly, the high-speed observer's velocity, and the curvature of spacetime. This investigation offers a more nuanced understanding of spectral shift anomalies in Sagnac interferometers, especially in scenarios involving significant velocities.

This work extends two earlier investigations on the parabolic adjoint operation within the Nilpotent Cone of the Langlands dual group in type $A$. Initially, we generalize the concept of Weierstrass sections to demonstrate its equivalence to a specific subset of the Nilpotent Cone. Subsequently, we identify a key component of the Nilpotent Cone as a direct product of irreducible representations associated with Weierstrass domains. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between components of the Nilpotent Cone and Weierstrass domains, potentially expanding the scope of future research in the area.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in certain tasks and are often on par with neural models when they are highly tuned. We investigated further and discovered that the primary advantage of neural models lies not in surpassing the $n$-gram base model but rather in their substantial model size. We developed a novel residual learning framework that allows the $n$-gram model to leverage the strengths of large language models while minimizing the need for large pretraining. Utilizing this framework across multiple datasets revealed that it yields substantial improvements in both parallel and sequential setup with minimal requirements for additional data and time. The significant benefits of the residual learning framework include reduced dependence on vast datasets and the ability to efficiently integrate new language models with minimal adjustments. Our research indicates that the $n$-gram model remains a viable option, and the simplicity of the residual learning framework makes it highly promising for various neural model applications.

We've developed new methods for analyzing $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial smooth varieties in positive characteristic using a combination of local uniformization and a generalization of Laurent's theorem. By extending these methods to non-smooth $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial varieties, we've discovered that such varieties can be expressed as the affine closure of a smooth variety defined by a set of binomial equations. Additionally, our approach allows us to prove a conjecture related to the study of $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial varieties.

Reconstructing and aligning 3D faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This study introduces a groundbreaking framework, Self-Aligned Dual Face Regression Networks, that tackles these challenges through two main innovations. Firstly, it employs a unique dual face regression approach, mapping images to descriptive codes that describe both the orientation and the three-dimensional shape of the face. Secondly, it utilizes an ingenious strategy to determine the orientation code automatically by identifying a latent alignment code embedded in the code representing the shape. This study also presents several challenging datasets featuring heavily occluded and orientationally diverse faces to evaluate the performance of its proposed method, which consistently outclasses existing techniques in face reconstruction tasks.

We demonstrate that the efficient descriptions of spacetime using differential forms lead to the discovery of fracton-like phenomena when the translation symmetry is arbitrarily slightly broken. The interconnection between the breakdown of translation symmetry and the fracton-like behavior is explicitly shown by utilizing the geometric formulation of differential forms. The subtle relationship between different breakdown modes of translation symmetry and various types of fractons is made clear. The scattering characteristics of the low-energy modes are found to be heavily constrained by the presence of fractons, with the result that the Euler characteristic of the spacetime manifold determines the dimensionality of the fracton branch. Furthermore, we illustrate that the differential form approach naturally yields theories with fusion rules for fractons, in addition to predicting that the density of states of systems featuring fractons will exhibit non-trivial behaviors as a function of energy. The potential of quantum gravity to be constrained by experiments through the study of the density of states is also raised.

In an $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, we examine the behavior of perturbations during the early stages of inflation and beyond the generation of primordial perturbations. By comparing academic estimates with actual cosmic microwave background measurements, we establish an upper limit for the model's parameters. Through numerical analysis, we identify potential areas of perturbation growth and oscillations due to the model's specific characteristics, such as the occurrence of Bardeen's regions. By further analyzing these regions, we determine the conditions under which the model could lead to the formation of black holes of a certain mass range, specifically in the range of $10^{15}$ to $10^{17}$ grams, and thus potentially account for the observed density of dark matter.

In this study, we first establish a clear distinction between two types of largest leaves in marked ordered trees: those located furthest from the root, and those with the longest downward path. We then extend this comparison to all deepest leaves by developing a recursive formula for the number of leaves at each distance level.

The accuracy of election outcomes depends on precise ballot tally readings, yet manual count validation is increasingly difficult due to the growing number of voting systems. This issue motivates the development of an enhanced optical character recognition system capable of learning from voting system data to reduce errors and improve count validation efficiency. This paper presents iOCR, a novel approach combining machine learning techniques to increase voting system data readability and optical character recognition accuracy. Our research demonstrates improved iOCR performance compared to existing methods using real-world data, showcasing its potential to enhance voting system data readability and automate count validation.

In the context of linear models, over-parameterization occurs when the number of model parameters exceeds the number of observed data points. Over-parameterization has been extensively studied in static data scenarios, but its implications for time series data remain under-explored. This paper delves into the consequences of over-parameterization in a time series setting, focusing on modeling real-time data using past observations. We demonstrate that a linear model with over-parameterization and restricted to a time series framework can achieve low generalization error without regularizers or significant data augmentation. This phenomenon holds true even when the model has many inactive features and significant slopes, and it is characterized by an o(n) bound on the prediction error. This result is further verified through numerical experiments and a survey of real-world applications. Additionally, an innovative strategy is presented for an over-parameterized model to approximate a hypothetical optimal model through data augmentation, and this approach is shown to lead to a more efficient use of data.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper presents a novel deep learning architecture called Complete Attention Bidirectional RNN for single-channel speech enhancement. This innovative model leverages attention mechanisms in both forward and reverse directions within a single recurrent neural network framework, enabling it to focus on specific time domain samples and make predictions. Compared to existing attention-based methods, this model demonstrates improved performance when tested with the DNS corpus, achieving notable gains in terms of signal-to-noise ratio.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack.

A key factor in microgrid functionality is the ability to store energy, but there are limitations to doing so due to risk aversion. This study analyzes how risk-averse storage systems affect decentralized energy pricing and self-allocation in a multi-agent model, utilizing a functional approach to handle uncertainty. It shows that risk-averse storage can impact pricing, but only through its impact on flexible resources. Furthermore, it indicates that optimal self-allocation is unbounded without consideration of storage limitations, but incorporating storage leads to a solution that involves the use of storage to hedge against uncertainty. This results in decreased demand for storage in some cases and increased prices for flexible resources.

In quantum systems, superpositions of electronic states rapidly evolve, 
within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the electronic dipole
