However, achieving inter-level coupling remains a challenge due to the complex quantum nature of this phenomenon. In our study, we successfully demonstrate inter-level coupling in a classical optical system using a laser source. This intervention effectively converts a system of non-interacting resonators into a quantum system characterized by Fock states. The associated Hamiltonian represents a universal platform for manipulating multiple modes at once, encompassing both dissipative and conservative interactions. Notably, our approach can also be applied to engineer the statistics of photon number distributions within these resonators.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Theoretical predictions for the masses of Ω-baryon states across various spin-parity configurations have been made available in the form of tables. A linear confining force also enables the derivation of magnetic moment values for these states.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our results to existing simpler models, we found that they often inaccurately predict infection risk, highlighting the need for more precise physical models, combined with future advancements in cough and sneeze simulations, to create reliable tools for evaluating transmission risks in urban buses and other enclosed environments.

Future high-energy accelerators like Higgs Factory or future linear colliders will likely reach energies where electron radiation in the vacuum surrounding the particle beam can cause diffraction, a phenomenon also known as quantum vacuum diffraction. This process is expected to result in birefringent effects on light emitted from these particles. To experimentally verify these effects, various detection methods have been proposed over the years. Our study evaluates and compares the feasibility of these detection methods using the parameters of the future Higgs Factory machine. The evaluation is based on the proposed experiment's sensitivity, with the goal of identifying the most viable methods for detecting quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence. Our analysis reveals that detecting these phenomena would require precise measurements of electron energy spectra and/or light intensity patterns. The most promising methods involve using magnetic spectrometers to measure electron energy spectra or light intensity distributions with the aid of thin layers with photoelectric properties. Alternatively, using hyperferfringent light to detect quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence has also been proposed. Our study shows that with the capabilities of future Higgs Factory-type machines, quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence can be detected with a relatively low number of required particles ($10^{11}$) and in a relatively short time frame (a few weeks).

In 1923, J.M. Eisenlohr and G.A. Farris developed a comprehensive approach to
identifying all possible combinations of edge lengths in fully transitive polyhedra.
Their method extends the earlier work by Bruckner, and it's a fundamental strategy
still utilized today. We'll examine the E-F method, detailing its key components
and illustrating its application with a specific example using a polyhedron with
8 triangular faces. This analysis will provide an in-depth look at the method's
underpinnings and its role in the current understanding of transitive polyhedra.

Building upon our previous work, we've developed novel uncloneable encryption schemes meeting the requirements set forth by Christopoulou and Hirt. Our new constructions incorporate both public key and private key scenarios, leveraging the concept of no-signaling measurement for quantum operations. We've also examined the feasibility of such schemes when combined with classical cryptography systems and investigated their key length requirements in both scenarios. Furthermore, we've identified the minimum number of qubits necessary for our schemes and explored potential applications using both single-use and reusable qubits.

This study proposes a novel approach to privately verifying the integrity of coded messages transmitted over noisy channels, without the need for a shared secret key between the encoder and verifier. The main contribution establishes a secure and efficient keyless verification protocol for polar codes, building on an earlier framework by Cramer et al. Additionally, this research develops a new security proof for polar codes in the real-world scenario, leveraging the properties of polarizing the uniform distribution. The findings also demonstrate the effectiveness of the keyless verification protocol through practical implementations and measurements.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate.

Both celestial bodies can experience massive losses due to an expansive outward flow of gas, often driven by energy expenditure or intense radiation. Additionally, powerful magnetic fields can shape this gas flow, creating a protective barrier around the body, while also allowing high-energy particles to pass through and interact with nearby external gas. If this external gas is dense enough, it can fuel an energetic particle wind, which in turn affects the magnetic field's configuration. The interaction between these processes can result in various phenomena, including blocked stellar radiation from filling its surrounding space with gas, inflated stellar magnetic fields pushed by high-energy particles, and gas flowing back towards its star due to magnetic connectivity. The understanding of these processes, though complex, can provide valuable insights into the physical properties of magnetized planetary bodies in distant celestial systems.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a more significant Spin-Orbit Coupling when a spin-polarized layer is proximized with a non-magnetic layer that has a large Spin-Orbit Coupling. In this study, we expressed the Spin-Orbit Coupling in a Bi/Co multilayer using the 4-band Kubo-Greenwood formula and found that the additional Spin-Orbit Coupling at the Bi interface enhances the orbital contribution. Furthermore, we discovered that the orbital contribution can be controlled through the strength of the interface interaction by adjusting the electric field. Our results indicate that the orbital contribution can be minimized, resulting in the pure spin effect, which is crucial for realizing the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalized Mie-type potential. The fractional version of the potential is defined as $\hat{H}\Psi(x_1,x_2,...,x_N)=\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}|x_i|^\alpha\right)^2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial |x_i|^{2\alpha}}+V(x_1,x_2,...,x_N)\right]\Psi(x_1,x_2,...,x_N)=E\Psi(x_1,x_2,...,x_N)$. By applying the Jumarie type fractional derivative, we obtain solutions in the form of $\Psi(x_1,x_2,...,x_N)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\omega t}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}C_n(\omega t)^n$. This expression enables the calculation of energy eigenvalues and corresponding wavefunction solutions for the generalized Mie-type potential.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be solved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularization. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their fundamental architecture relies on learning sequential patterns from input sequences.
In the context of agglutinative languages like Basque, word morphology follows a specific pattern.
It is intriguing to investigate whether a simple neural network can learn this pattern just by seeing the sequence of a word's syllables.
In this paper, a straightforward approach using an LSTM network is tested to see if it can learn the Bassque conformance rule.
The study's innovative aspect lies in its comparison of two extermely dissimilar evaluation frameworks.
It demonstrates that the proposed method's performance is comparable even when using a less optimal evaluation framework.
The analysis of the findings suggests that neural networks are capable of learning the Basque conformance rule.
In addition, the study evaluates the impact of several factors on the model's performance.
It shows that neural networks are robust to changes in suffix order and are most effective when given a fully written Basque word.
The analysis of the findings is further validated by a key aspect, i.e., the role of the neural network's internal state.
It is demonstrated that the neural network's performance is closely linked to its initial state.
In conclusion, the study holds significant implications for the further exploration of neural networks in context-free rule-based models.
It also paves the way for studying the application of neural networks in languages with complex phonology and morphology.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow researchers to detect subtle irregularities in the planet's orbit when combined with upcoming observations using the James Webb Space Telescope.

Foundations games such as Chess, Bingo, and Tic-Tac-Toe have proven effectiveness in providing enjoyable experiences for users of varying skill levels. To understand how to successfully introduce an opponent, a survey of 150 participants was conducted, analyzing the perceived competitiveness of various game states. A theoretical framework was then developed to classify game states as easy to win from, difficult to win from, drawn, or won, using the concepts of "zone of control" and "degree of control". This framework can be applied to design intuitive and engaging experiences for users, especially in the context of physical rehabilitation, by utilizing the principles of foundations gameplay to create motivating challenges that promote a sense of accomplishment and reduce frustration.

This research introduces an energy-based variational model that incorporates a piecewise-rigid map representation to solve surface reconstruction problems with discontinuities. By leveraging the Ambrosio-Tortorelli approximation, a nonconvex and singular model is formulated and existence proved through compactness and convergence arguments, yielding a piecewise-rigid surface reconstruction. A numerical model based on the proposed variational model is also presented and exemplified through computational experiments.

We investigate the production of lepton-quark pairs at the LHC within the context of third-generation vector leptoquark models, focusing on the Drell-Yan process. To achieve this, we calculate precise corrections to their production and decay, taking into account the impact of QCD. To ensure accuracy, we apply these corrections at the next-to-leading order in QCD. Additionally, we account for multiple hadronizations, incorporating precise parton shower corrections. Our analysis is particularly relevant in scenarios where the leptoquark mass significantly exceeds the colliding energy, in which case the pair production of the vector leptoquarks dominates the signal. Furthermore, we examine the effect of integrating our predictions with parton shower algorithms and find them to be consistent with existing implementations. We also derive precise corrections to the pair production of the vector leptoquarks decaying into a bottom-quark and a muon or electron pair. These findings are made available in the form of a validated Monte Carlo event generator.

We have designed a novel neural network framework that is sensitive to physical properties and varies in its prediction outcomes when given different input images. This uncertainty quantification allows our model to identify and disregard images with abnormal PET images based on CT images. By filtering out images that are likely inaccurate due to low dose levels, our model can make more accurate predictions for PET images taken at lower doses. We tested our approach with a realistic simulation of whole-body PET scans and confirmed that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques using current low-dose PET data. Additionally, our model demonstrated improved performance when tested with artificially created out-of-distribution data.

Personalization is ubiquitous in modern technology, and users regularly surrender their data in exchange for tailored experiences. Despite the widespread acceptance of personalization, users still harbor privacy concerns and demonstrate a desire for customization options free from intrusive data collection. This study's primary goal is to gain insight into users' attitudes towards personalization and privacy. It presents an appeal-based personalization system, where users volunteer demographic and interest information in exchange for customized content. The analysis of collected data reveals users' willingness to balance privacy and personalization, and how they compare to existing research findings. The data indicates that users are more open to data collection when there are tangible benefits, but still value their anonymity. Additionally, the study confirms previous research discoveries regarding age-related differences in users' attitudes towards personalization and privacy. It also explores potential design strategies for an appeal-based system, and highlights areas for further research into the topic.

This research investigates the relationship between centering theory and coreference resolution. Initially, we analyzed the interrater variability in annotated data to determine the average distance between human raters and a state-of-the-art coreference resolution model. Subsequently, we examined the prediction capabilities of the same model in identifying certain key features associated with centering, including their level of accuracy and utility in further refining coreference resolution. Additionally, we explored the potential for feature-based neural network models to surpass the existing coreference resolution system, finding them to perform similarly or slightly worse than the original model. Nonetheless, our findings suggest there is room for improvement in neural coreference resolution systems, especially when incorporating centering features.

A graph is considered upward planar if a planar drawing of the graph can be found such that all edges radiate clockwise around every vertex. This property is maintained even after the introduction of linear orderings for the vertices. We examine various parameters such as number of sources, number of sinks, number of leaves in a tree-decomposition, and we establish specific parameters that can be solved in polynomial time for detecting upward planarity. We also provide a non-fpt algorithm for solving the problem with a linear number of leaves in a tree-decomposition. Furthermore, we introduce new ftmber functions that can be solved efficiently for detecting upward planarity. We also investigate the suitability of specific parameters such as treewidth, branchwidth, and treedepth in solving the problem efficiently.

The rising intricacy of modern automated systems demands significant setup time from experts, necessitating a automated setup process. To this end, a setup framework is proposed that detects configuration issues through continuous system monitoring and automatic testing. It localizes the source of the problem, generates a corrective action, and executes it to resolve the issue. The proposed method is utilized in the development of the HaNet framework, a system designed for human robot interaction experiments. HaNet features multiple robots, sensory equipment, and a range of objects that need to be placed in a particular arrangement. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through its implementation on HaNet, highlighting the importance of clear and concise documentation to support automated setup processes.

The average growth of a given set of operators in the Hilbert space is often evaluated using the standard operator growth theory. This approach has been successfully applied to various systems, including non-interacting systems, random quantum systems, and systems at criticality. In such cases, the operator growth follows a specific quadratic or linear pattern. However, there are some complex systems where the connection between different operators is not well understood. These systems require a more refined analysis that takes into account the correlation between different operators. In our study, we examine the operator operator correlation in systems at criticality and in the GKPSI phase, and compare it to the operator density. Our results show that the correlation between different operators can be very high, often exceeding 0.9. Notably, in the GKPSI phase, the average correlation between operators in the $i^{th}$ block and those in the $10^{th}$ block is significantly higher than in the $i^{th}$ block and those in the $i^{th}$ block itself. This phenomenon may explain the slow decay of operator density with increasing distance. Additionally, we find that the correlation between operators in the $i^{th}$ block and those in the $10^{th}$ block is remarkably high in the SU(4) spin liquid, despite the much greater density of operators in the $10^{th}$ block. This suggests that the operator growth in this system is highly non-local.

Recently, WiFi-based range estimation has gained significant interest as it offers a convenient and economical method for determining distances in various settings. This interest is driven by the advancement of technology and growing reliance on WiFi signals, which are now ubiquitous. Ultimately, implementing this technique could revolutionize traditional distance measuring methods. However, existing research on WiFi-based range estimation is limited, which is why we are investigating this topic. Our analysis focuses on comparing the performance of different machine learning algorithms in estimating ranges. In our experiment, we selected a random sample of 500 data points from each of the 5 floors in a large office building, which resulted in accurately predicting ranges on 4 out of 5 floors but struggled with the 5th floor. Notably, our findings revealed that certain features have a negative impact on predictions, which is an novel observation in this field. To achieve the best results, we identified certain hyperparameters that yield the most accurate predictions. Our analysis also highlighted potential issues with signal fluctuation affecting results. Ultimately, our research paves the way for further exploration of WiFi-based range estimation, while also highlighting the importance of carefully selecting features and considering the physical environment in which the technique is being implemented.

In 1960, Freeman Dyson used the concept of an infinite array of spacecraft to define a region in space that indicates the level of advanced civilization development. We explore the possibility of Dyson Shells surrounding a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy by examining various potential appearances of these shells using newly updated observations from the Hubble Space Telescope. Our research focuses on five nearby galaxies containing active black holes, for a total of 12 Dyson Shell candidates. Although we were unable to rule out the possibility that some of these shells are being inhabited by advanced civilizations, our study reveals that constructing a Dyson Shell around a black hole would require a civilization with a level of energy output comparable to the brightest stars in the galaxy. Our findings also suggest that in galaxies similar to the Milky Way, there would only be enough accessible energy to build a Dyson Shell within a radius of approximately 10 parsecs, or about 32 light-years, around the black hole.

Network applications rely heavily on service quality, which is safeguarded by Service Level Agreements (SLAs). Ensuring SLA compliance is crucial for both users and providers. A robust SLA monitoring system is necessary to achieve this, but traditional approaches to performance monitoring, based on centralized methods, are prone to failures. In contrast, a decentralized performance monitoring system, built using peer-to-peer (P2P) technology, can provide a more reliable solution. We examine the potential benefits of decentralization for identifying SLA violations and outline a reference architecture for a decentralized SLA monitoring system. However, a detailed analysis of implementation specifics and associated costs remains a topic for further research.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling design, energy gain per turn, and recirculation number on beam breakup instability. This paper examines the effect of filling design on beam breakup instability in multi-pass energy recovery linacs, with considerations for real-world applications where beam properties may vary across different passes. A theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrate that beam breakup instability can be influenced by fill design, especially in multi-pass accelerators. The findings suggest that, with proper design, beam breakup instability can be managed, and high current multi-pass beams achieved. The research also identifies potential strategies for optimizing beam performance through filling design, including machine design and operating protocols.

To determine resonance neutron energies, precise neutron detection is crucial. The statistical uncertainty of neutron time-of-flight data is often limited by the total neutron cross-section, especially below 10 MeV. To address this, we developed a novel 3D scintillator sensor using a TPC design for accurate neutron counting and energy measurement. By utilizing this sensor in a neutron time-of-flight experiment at the FRM-II research reactor, we successfully measured the total neutron cross-section on carbon with a relative uncertainty of 0.5-4.5%, potentially enabling the identification of neutron resonances below 10 MeV.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth.

This R package provides functions for performing Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA), a localized adaptation of the Fisher Discriminant Analysis (FDA) technique. The package also includes methods for visualizing LFDA components and related graphs. Additionally, it offers tools for creating 3D plots of data using the lfda3d function, which utilizes the plot3d package. Furthermore, the package is designed with efficiency in mind, utilizing sparse matrix operations to enhance its speed. A recent improvement to the package includes the ability to handle missing data through the use of the KFold method.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental interactions, imitation learning can produce more refined results by considering which actions are permissible given the robot's setup and surrounding objects. However, conventional methods fail to effectively capture complex constraints, often requiring the modification of demonstration trajectories or the relaxation of strict standards. To address these limitations, we introduce an extended variant of maximum likelihood estimation, EKMP, capable of handling multi-dimensional demonstrations, non-linear constraints, and obstacle avoidance. In a comparative study involving synthetic and real-world data, our extended framework demonstrates superior performance compared to baseline methods.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

A novel kind of topological superfluid that has a spinless character has been discovered in a Huband model that contains a Rashba interaction. This finding is especially notable because the Rashba interaction, a type of orbital interaction that causes rotation, typically hinders the formation of a spinless topological superfluid. Our study reveals that this counterintuitive result occurs due to a unique balance of forces that favor the rotation of atoms in pairs, a phenomenon that could be located within an experimental reachable range of temperatures and densities. This research was conducted on an optical disk-shaped trap that simulates the effects of rotation on paired atoms through a technique called mean field theory. Our analysis shows that both pair formation and topological feature persist even when the intensity of the Rashba interaction is increased, a phenomenon that could be understood by examining the energy levels of a pair of atoms in a harmonic potential. This finding is especially notable because the Rashba interaction, a type of orbital interaction that causes rotation, typically hinders the formation of a spinless topological superfluid. By precisely measuring the magnetization of upturned Cu wires in doped La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{8}$, we have observed a distinctive grid-like arrangement of vortex lines at sufficiently low external magnetic field. This phenomenon is notable because it represents a rare instance of directly observed vortex phase transition in magnetic properties measured during a change in external field. Our research reveals that the vortex line arrangement changes from a rectangular to a square pattern as the sample is moved from the 'up' to the 'down' orientation, and this occurrence is linked to the angular anisotropy of the superconducting gap in the material.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a new class of models, incorporating a distinct 'exclusion zone' dimension. Nonetheless, the dimensions of this 'exclusion zone' have not been clearly defined. In this study, a novel, arbitrary-shape brush model is presented, involving the precise 'exclusion zone' dimension, and validated through numerical simulations of curved, stretched brushes. The results show that the 'exclusion zone' dimension correlates strongly with the fluctuation radius of gyration in brush regimes, particularly in the asymptotic regime of low surface curvatures. Nonetheless, in the case of strongly stretched brushes on the faces of spherical substrates, the 'exclusion zone' dimension deviates from this scaling, instead following a larger power law. Additionally, the findings indicate that the dimensions of the 'exclusion zone' have a significant impact on the overall scaling of the brush's characteristic radius, particularly in the regime of low surface curvatures. Consequently, the proposed model offers a comprehensive explanation for the enhanced thickness of brushes located within depressions, a phenomenon initially attributed to comb-like chain fluctuations.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A minimal identifying set is one with the fewest points. The minimum size of such a set is the metric dimension of a graph. Here we discuss the version of this concept using the trimmed version of a distance measure.

Researchers explored the use of machine learning algorithms to analyze all-sky maps created from a year's worth of data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. By training a convolutional neural network on these maps, they were able to enhance the detection of gamma-ray sources and identify variables across the sky. Comparing the results to conventional methods, they found the machine learning approach was effective at detecting known sources and surpassing the sensitivity of current techniques for detecting variable sources. Additionally, it was found that many of the sources considered non-variable by traditional methods actually showed some level of variability.

A serial dictatorship is a method for making choices when there is agreement that cannot be reached, using the preferences of the individuals involved. It is based on the idea that the order in which the people's preferences are considered makes a difference, as does the fact that some individuals' opinions may carry more weight than others. A key aspect of a serial dictatorship is the order in which the people's preferences are considered, which is determined by the irreflexive and transitive nature of the relationships between the individuals. The weight that each person's opinions carry is also a key factor, which is typically represented by the strength of the relationships between the individuals. 

The formula for calculating the optimal order has been the focus of existing research, particularly on its computational aspects, but the study of the optimal rule based on the formula has been overlooked until now. The weight that each person's opinions carry, which is represented by the strength of the relationships between the individuals, can be seen as a measure of their type of preference. 

In this study, we are looking for the rule that chooses the optimal order, given the people's preferences, and we call this rule the strong serial dictatorship (SSD). But first, we need to identify the conditions under which the optimal order can be determined uniquely, and we call these conditions the strong serial dictatorship (SSD) profile.

We present initial findings from a comprehensive examination of binary asters, 
also known as binary stars with nearly equal brightness, conducted across various 
spectral types and in multiple directions from the Sun. This study is based on 
photometric data collected by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope between 2010 and 2019, 
and involving up to 5 different optical filters. Our analysis includes a 
robust detection process, removal of false positives, and consideration of various 
constraints such as the characteristics of the detector and the movement of the 
stars across the image frame. Ultimately, our research yielded a notable result: 
for the Sun's movement across the sky, there is a notable disparity in the number 
of binary asters detected with low motion speeds, especially among the coolest 
spectral types. This finding is particularly significant as it may have implications 
for existing theories regarding the properties of cool binary stars. To better 
understand these results, we have developed various techniques to review the data 
firsthand, examine potential distractions in the photometric records, and assess 
the performance of our detection tools. Additionally, we have outlined a key 
scientific question that could benefit from further investigation.

This research extends the conventional partial linear model by incorporating network data and establishing new theoretical bounds for consistent estimation and hypothesis testing. Initially, we establish a new representation of the partial linear model in a network setting. Subsequently, we develop a consistent estimation procedure based on a novel representation and demonstrate its validity under specific conditions. Additionally, we derive a theoretical framework for conducting inferences in a network context. Notably, our study also explores a notable example involving peer influence within networks.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for these operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas obtained from the product rule, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper examines how a sophisticated detection system, utilizing an adaptive filter based on the least squares method, is able to detect signals with characteristics that differ across space. We develop a theoretical framework to predict the performance of this system, and through computational simulations, verify that it is effective in scenarios where the signals have distinct patterns. Furthermore, we show that it can outperform traditional detection methods based on matched filters.

We've developed an open-source suite of web tools to support the use of representation learning for spectroscopic and imaging data. These tools provide intuitive interfaces for users to explore representation learning's potential applications and provide access to necessary supporting data. As representation learning's effectiveness is often evaluated using metrics like likelihood and classification accuracy, we've incorporated features to easily compute these metrics alongside visualizations of model predictions. To facilitate collaboration and reproducibility, we've incorporated an interface for users to replicate previous analysis and results. Furthermore, we've established a data repository that hosts spectroscopic and imaging datasets, along with associated metadata, to support representation learning. This suite of tools is designed to streamline the process of exploring new methods for representation learning.

The Southern Atlantic rift underwent a complex division of Africa and South America as the two continents moved apart over millions of years. Various studies have attempted to analyze the rift's kinematics, yet a detailed, polynomial-based model of the process has not been established. Our research presents a comprehensive, 250 million-year extension model spanning from 104 Ma to present, focusing on the changes in rotation, radius of curvature, and half-width of the basin. A multi-parameter, least-squares minimization approach revealed a set of optimal values for b, c, and d, characteristic of the rift's geometry. A notable shift in extension direction occurred at 87.4 Ma, coinciding with the lessening of rifting acceleration. A change in rotation rate around the Atlantic axis became evident at 56.2 Ma, associated with altered sea floor production and temperature changes in the supercontinent Gondwana.

A proven strategy to enhance segmentation without labeled data is unsupervised unscaled cross-entropy training, but it has limitations such as being boundary-sensitive and relying on initial guesses. Another approach, unsupervised contrastive learning, has demonstrated great potential but mainly focuses on learning general image characteristics and often ignores medical image-specific knowledge. Integrating these methods can help to overcome their individual drawbacks. We present an novel framework that combines two methods to address these challenges. In our framework, we first use an modified unsupervised contrastive learning approach that incorporates a more precise contrastive loss function and integrates medical image-specific knowledge. We then incorporate a novel boundary-augmentation technique inspired by Fourier transformation to augment segmentations. By conducting extensive experiments on real-world datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/zwang-buaa/SMIC-ISM.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared intent.

Understanding the meaning of words is foundational to any language-based knowledge represents a fundamental challenge in building robust, general knowledge bases. Word sense induction (WSI) aims to systematically identify and categorize the varied meanings of words. Although significant progress has been made in recent years, the full potential of WSI in enriching knowledge bases has yet to be realized. This paper introduces a novel approach to WSI centered on semantic variation discovery, where the focus is on identifying the differences in meaning among words, rather than their individual interpretations. This approach is designed to be more efficient and effective, as evidenced by superior performance in comparative evaluations of three major WSI datasets. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called Bilingual Lexical Semantic Variations (BLSV), comprising 1,000 pairs of languages, along with 1 million word instances, to represent the diverse meanings of words. This dataset poses a significant challenge for WSI, as it requires the discovery of differences in meaning across multiple words and languages.

We propose a new set of distribution functions for quasiparticles within the kernel perp-dependent quasiparticle approximation, ensuring positive occupation probabilities and detailed balance, thus maintaining the stability of in-medium particle properties. This leads to an explicit expression for the Wigner function, connecting the distribution functions to spectral functions, and establishing a correlation between the kernel perp-dependent quasiparticle approximation and the JIM-WAM model. Our approach also facilitates an interpretation of the kernel perp-dependent quasiparticle approximation as a special case of the JIM-WAM model, defined through a convolution based on the Bessel function.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and folding processes is not yet fully understood. Research suggests that knotted protein structures may utilize specific folding pathways to compensate for energy barriers caused by self-interference. To explore this concept, we developed a quantum simulation of knotted peptide chains in motion, incorporating their native states and relying on a topological framework to identify compatible bending pathways. Our analysis reveals that in most cases, compatible pathways are readily available, often tracing the perimeter of the knot with little resistance. However, there are exceptions, demonstrating that knots can also present insurmountable obstacles to folding, and leading us to propose a new measure of a protein's knottiness that predicts its ability to fold through smooth pathways. This measurement shows a strong correlation with experimental data, indicating that some proteins are naturally resistant to folding due to complex knot structures.

To resolve the discrepancy between theoretical predictions and actual galaxy spin observations, we tested early dark energy models using the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's galaxy data. By creating a profile likelihood function and calculating its value for each model, we determined the parameters' ranges that fit the data well. According to our results, the range in which the data is a good fit is more restrictive than previously thought, particularly in regards to the parameter a that indicates how much early dark energy contributes to the density of the universe. Specifically, a must be less than 0.016 in order for the data to make sense. This limitation holds true regardless of how we model the growth of galaxy clusters and does not conflict with the results from other experiments that are yet to be analyzed thoroughly.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is conducted, with a focus on its underlying assumptions within the context of both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. The study utilizes a categorical framework to simultaneously explore both theoretical domains. The conditions that yield a NG phenomenon are examined, with an analysis of the implications of vacuum stability in relation to the presence or absence of a NG phenomenon. The role of the symmetry in the NG phenomenon is also investigated, with a consideration of both direct and indirect symmetries. Theoretical models, including those with broken Lorentz symmetry, nonrelativistic symmetry, and quantum electrodynamics, are used to illustrate the principles discussed. The work aims to provide an exhaustive explanation of the NG phenomenon in quantum field theories.

Recent studies indicate that models based on language, when trained with superset data that includes pseudo-labels, can learn to improve their performance. Nonetheless, the reliance on labeling data raises concerns of cost, efficiency, and bias. Our proposed approach, distilling phrasal hypotheses with language models, aims to minimize the need for labeling. We utilize a method called knowledge-assisted data augmentation that leverages a knowledge base to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for regions in sentences that are difficult to process. We develop a knowledge graph-based dataset, titled Phrasel, which comprises a set of phrasal hypotheses derived from sections of scientific articles. Our evaluation reveals that models based on language can effectively learn from a significantly reduced subset of labeled data, resulting in a 15% improvement in overall performance. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that models based on language can achieve comparable performance to specialized models when trained on a reduced subset of labeled data, specifically outperforming them by 10% when trained on 10% of the data.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs. Our findings apply to the integers 2 and 3 when the circulant graph satisfies particular degree and connection criteria. Additionally, our results include instances where the total chromatic number is equivalent to one and two times the number of vertices in the circulant graph, respectively.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique pinhole pattern due to local strain. This finding suggests that very small defects in the graphene or changes in surface energy could steer Heusler film growth between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. It also reveals that clean graphene surfaces offer little advantage over oxide substrates, and that surface energy is the dominant controlling factor in these processes. As a result, future research should focus not only on developing clean, contamination-free graphene growth environments, but also on manipulating surface energy through various methods to ensure successful remote epitaxy.

This paper delves into the study of $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, initially presented in a previous work, where we introduced the concept and examined its ranking in terms of maximum dimension for a specific code length. In this continuation, we expand the study by determining the dimension of arbitrary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes and confirming that a particular subclass of these codes meets the criteria of GRS codes, while also identifying the kernel of the encoding and decoding functions.

The functionality of a polymer plug in fluid characterization is determined by an optimal injection profile that is inherently symmetrical. By assuming that the rock's properties remain constant and considering only single-phase flow, we have analytically determined the optimal polymer plug profile that maximizes the subject-area integral by scaling the polymer injection rate according to the square root of the distance from the injection point. Additionally, we have derived an explicit formula for the optimal polymer profile when there is two-phase flow with Caffeine as the non-surfactant fluid. Our research provides the foundation for investigating how different injection profiles impact the efficiency of various polymer applications, including EOR (Enhanced Oil Recovery) techniques.

No-tensor models have been the preferred choice for structured output domains due to their computational efficiency and ease of optimization. Nonetheless, most no-tensor models have limited success when dealing with multi-label classification tasks. For instance, simple frequency lists significantly outperform the current state-of-the-art models for zero-shot multi-label classification. Zashkin et al. attribute this success to the fact that frequency lists embody a refined version of the underlying output distribution. Based on this assumption, we develop a novel approach to refine the output distribution by extracting multi-label samples from single positive labels. Our proposed framework, which incorporates a new type of self-supervised learning objective, allows for the acquisition of refined output instances by drawing upon existing negative examples. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving superior performance on various multi-label classification tasks, including zero-shot and supervised settings, according to extensive experimental evaluations conducted on multiple datasets.

This study investigates the energy dissipation property of the time-fractional
Allen-Cahn equation, introducing a new upper bound that diminishes over time.
Existing works typically establish non-increasing energy functions, often relying
on the equation's weak form or the compactness of the embedding of the underlying
space. In contrast, this research is set apart by its utilization of the strong
form of the equation. A novel feature of this study is the derivation of an explicit
energy function, which is a scalar expression rather than a norm. Building upon
these findings, the research is extended to the time-fractional Cahn-Hemontier equation.

The relationship between physical states and observable quantities is governed by the principle of the correspondence, which posits that the former's equivalence or similarity implies the latter's equivalence or similarity, and conversely. This study's first main contribution is to provide a categorical framework that explicitly captures this relationship, and its underlying assumption is a category of physical systems that is equipped with structure in the form of a symplectic form, a symplectic state space, and a map that relates states to observables. The second main contribution is to demonstrate that this categorical framework can be derived from either the category of classical systems or the category of quantum systems. The study also explores the derived category of quantum systems in detail, and it reveals that it is a category of Hilbert spaces that is equipped with structure in the form of a symplectic form, a symplectic state space, and a map that relates states to observables. This study's results imply that the category of quantum systems is not equivalent to the category of Hilbert spaces because the latter lacks the correspondence between states and observables. The study's findings also raise the question of whether it is possible to construct a derived category of physical systems that is free from any underlying assumption, and whether such a category would be equivalent to the category of von Neumann algebras.

The source of very-high-energy gamma-rays in nearby radio galaxies has long been an intriguing mystery. We propose that gamma-rays are produced when magnetic fields in the disks around supermassive black holes restrict the formation of powerful particle jets, instead creating a different type of jet that travels at a slower speed due to being slowed down by the grid of the gravitational potential around the black hole. This model suggests that a specific alignment is necessary for such a jet to point towards Earth, and takes this into account to predict which gamma-ray sources are likely to be associated with a particular orientation. Our simulation shows that a significant number of gamma-ray blazars can be accounted for with this model, and that the energy of the gamma-rays can be explained by a high energy process occurring in the disk, although being influenced by the magnetic field. It also suggests that a search for such restricted jets should be identifiable by their lower speed, which could be confirmed by future telescopes capable of observing the motion of such jets.

This study presents a new approach to evaluating portfolio performances based on their rankings among all possible portfolios, established through their relationship with a specified set of assets. The performance of each portfolio is determined by its ranking, R, where higher rankings indicate better performance. A key feature of this method is the use of a ranking function that defines the overall performance of a portfolio by considering all possible outcomes of its R ranking. The study introduces an explicit formula for the expected return of a specific portfolio type and shows how the method can be applied to answer a range of questions, including identifying the optimal portfolio that maximizes expected return, estimating the probability of a portfolio performing better than another, and ranking portfolios based on their performance.

This study involves categorizing heart sounds into normal and abnormal based on their acoustic properties, with considerations for external noise and the distortion caused by cardiac device implants. A neural network was designed and tested for various combinations of noise and distortion, with initial development using noise-free data and comparisons made for different levels of noise and distortion. The findings showed that even high levels of noise and severe distortion can still allow for accurate classification. The designed network was also compared to a traditional Fourier transform approach, with the results indicating a significant improvement in accuracy. Furthermore, the findings suggested that the Fourier transform approach can be sensitive to cardiac device implants, with classifications based on implant type being consistently accurate when using this method.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This study introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth aggregates data via a federated approach, leveraging transfer learning to develop personalized models. The framework comprises three main components, including a data preparation section where data is sorted into chronological order and normalized to standardize unit measurements. Subsequently, the federated learning section builds models using a variant of the Federated Averaging algorithm, adapted for healthcare datasets. Lastly, the transfer learning section utilizes hard parameter sharing to develop personalized models. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.03% greater accuracy compared to conventional personalized approaches, and the framework is available online at https://github.com/armandoshj/FedHealth.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance, therefore, cannot persist forever, and the chance 
exists that we reside in the universe's first epoch. Our quintessence model illustrates the 
dysfunctional universe dynamics resulting from the descent of heavy states, when a multitude of particles 
are produced, overshadowing the quintessence's power. Additionally, our theory raises implications 
for the universe's early inflationary periods.

The rapid evolution of software applications leads to significant issues with maintaining existing tools for software testing and debugging. Moreover, the lack of standardization in technologies and languages complicates attempts to create universally applicable tools. In response to these challenges, researchers are exploring the use of general-purpose machine learning models that can tackle a wide range of tasks without requiring specific domain knowledge. In this paper, we investigate the potential benefits of applying such models to automate various tasks in software development, testing, and maintenance. By drawing on recent studies and examples from popular open-source projects, we highlight the advantages of this approach and outline the promising outcomes it produces, finally identifying key challenges and potential areas for future work.

This study explores a complex issue in optimal control theory, where the costs of transitioning between states are subject to significant discontinuities. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal control strategy using various techniques. We demonstrate that by applying a specific method, the solution can be expressed as a combination of policies that switch between different state occupancy levels. Furthermore, this method provides a practical means of approximating the optimal solution numerically. Another key finding is that under certain conditions, the optimal control can be represented as a set of continuous state occupancy levels. We also establish a connection between the optimal control problem and a related issue involving the minimum of a collection of functions. Specifically, we show that the optimal control strategy can be obtained by identifying the most disruptive change within a specific group of functions and selecting the state that leads to the largest impact. This achievement requires the costs of transitioning between states to be distinct.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates various scalar leptoquark combinations that could contribute to discrepancies in certain high-energy processes. Focusing on the process of unequal leptoquark pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, we investigate the impact of initial state radiation and colliding parton energies. Additionally, our analysis considers the effects of leptoquark interactions within the Standard Model and beyond. With anti-parallel leptoquark decays, our findings reveal that even when interacting with first generation quarks and electrons, a 1000 GeV leptoquark mass can result in unequal pair production leading to an invariant mass spectrum with notable features, including a sharp end and a distinct dip around 200 GeV, that could be distinctive enough to set limits on leptoquark mass through data analysis. Furthermore, our study discovers that with anti-parallel leptoquark decays, the choice of leptoquark charge and nature has a significant impact on final state particle identification, effectively allowing for the elimination of certain leptoquark combinations based on equal pair production data analysis.

This study proposes a novel guided learning approach to capture the temporal evolution of biological samples using few-dimensional data. The framework utilizes meta-learning to develop highly flexible models that can effectively utilize limited, high-dimensional temporal sequence data to predict key outcome measures. The team applied this approach to two challenging problems: predicting cell death rates based on gene expression levels and forecasting patient response to different doses of cytokine treatment in a biochemical system. Results showed the guided learning framework outperformed traditional state-of-the-art methods using data from the Model Cell and BioFactory systems. The team observed that the model's ability to generalize from limited data was surprising, especially considering the significantly larger dimensionality of unguided learning. The proposed framework shows promise for predicting critical outcomes in complex biological systems with minimal data requirements.

We analyze the CIA lines of chlorine at 1.532 $\mu$m and 1.765 $\mu$m to understand their excitation in molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies. By examining 21 cm line data and far-infrared continuum observations of galactic centers, we investigate the correlation between CIA emission and other physical properties of galaxies. Our results show a weak correlation between CIA emission and the thermal kinetic pressure of gas in galaxy centers. By contrast, there is a strong correlation between CIA emission and the thermal kinetic pressure of gas in the broader molecular disks of galaxies. This latter relationship holds true even when controlling for factors like star formation rate, gas mass, and galactic mass. Interestingly, the excitation of CIA lines is found to be subthermal in molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies on average, with an average degree of thermalization less than 0.5. This finding suggests a limitation on the energy available for heating gas in galaxy centers and broader molecular disks. By exploring the potential utility of CIA lines as an indicator of gas excitation, we examine the advantages and limitations of using these lines in place of other tracers.

The observed excesses of $B$-decays and precision parity-violating observables can be simultaneously explained through a framework that involves heavy vectorlike particles that are only visible in the strong force. To achieve this, these particles must be part of a larger set of heavy vectorlike states that are coupled to the top quark in a specific way. As a result, the top quark's anomalous couplings are affected, leading to predictions that can be tested in future experiments. Through a thorough exploration of the available parameter space, we have identified the most constraining experiments and found that some may need to consider new background contributions. Furthermore, we have found that the predicted excesses in $B$-decays can also be addressed through the same type of vectorlike states that are also responsible for the parity-violating anomalies. However, this requires additional, more restrictive conditions on the underlying physics.

Levenshtein initially explored the sequence reconstruction problem using the Hamming distance, focusing on permutations with a specific distance threshold. This paper delves deeper into permutations with a Hamming distance of at least $k$ by examining the minimum number of distinguishing positions required. We present a constructive proof that this number is less than or equal to $k$, and through further analysis, we identify certain upper and lower bounds for specific values of $k$. These bounds reveal that when $k$ equals $1$, the minimum number is $1$, and for $k$ greater than $1$, the minimum number is $k$, indicating that sequences with a Hamming distance of at least $k$ can be distinguished using fewer than $k$ distinguishing positions only when $k$ is $2$.

Research in using deep learning for identifying musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance a prototypical network with a hierarchical loss function and a parental pointer module in order to incorporate an instrument's place in the hierarchy. This is done by adding a parental pointer module to the network's latent representation, enabling it to draw inspiration from parental classes. The proposed method is then tested on a dataset consisting of 30 categories, for which there's limited data available in each category. The results show that the method's capacity to learn from a limited number of examples makes it particularly suitable for few-shot learning scenarios.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek answers to several questions but typically ask only a few. To facilitate more in-depth reading, we developed a new research paper comprehension standard and a comprehensive dataset called PMQ, consisting of over 10,000 question-answer pairs related to twelve diverse research areas. Each question is designed to elicit information missing from the corresponding paper, and more than 90% of participating PhD researchers and industry professionals deemed the answers novel when confronted with the associated paper. PMQ is now publicly accessible to foster innovative ideas and inspire new areas of study.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow bandwidth scenarios. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within the current PTA sensitivity limits.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on particles moving in a linear gradient context. By solving the equation, we find the wavefunction of the ground state and calculate key physical properties, ultimately determining the energy spectrum, wavefunction behavior, and probability distribution within a one-dimensional harmonic potential well. Additionally, we investigate spin behavior and correlation phenomena. Results show an irregular energy spectrum, ground state normalization, and abnormal probability distribution. Furthermore, we find spin behavior correlation and an irregular distribution within a one-dimensional harmonic potential well.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of a process that transforms spin-polarized atoms into atom-molecule pairs using a single laser beam. This process begins with two interacting spin-polarized atoms that are trapped and cooled to sub-millikelvin temperatures. We examine how a far-off-resonance laser affects their behavior, considering both its effects on the relative motion of the atoms and a two-body interaction that arises from the combination of the laser's field and a distant resonance. We found that by controlling the intensity of the laser, it is possible to select the atomic pair's initial state and ultimately achieve a transition from two fermionic atoms to a molecular bond. The conditions required for this transition to occur are critically dependent on the pair's initial state. For instance, in the case of two paired up spins, a moderate laser intensity is sufficient; however, for two paired down spins, a much more intense laser is needed. The process of atom-molecule transformation can also be achieved through the interaction of three atoms, where two of the atoms are in an entangled spin state and a third atom is in an unentangled spin state. This process results in a molecule formed through a two-body interaction between two atoms that are in an entangled spin state. We found that in this case, a much more complex relationship exists between the laser intensity required and the initial conditions of the atoms. Furthermore, this process may potentially be used to create a quantum state that cannot be achieved through other methods.

Our proposed DNA-storage support structure provides efficient support for inserting data into a hierarchical format on DNA. This code has been successfully tested with a range of data sets, including those with linear, binary, and multi-level hierarchies. A performance comparison shows our method outperforms existing DNA storage solutions by up to 89.01 and 23.08 in insertion efficiency for linear and hierarchical data respectively.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered images, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations and parallel lighting to achieve visibility consideration with minimal additional computation, transforming parallel lighting into differentiable multi-light shading. Building on this foundation, we develop a differentiable shadow computation method that employs spherical harmonics and lighting visibility, enabling the solution of frontals-only image-based inverse problems with significant improvements in accuracy and convergence speed.

A prominent issue in video playback is the interlacing effect, which causes horizontal lines of a frame to be captured sequentially. This problem is addressed by implementing a motion estimation technique, however existing methods often struggle to balance processing speed and level of detail. Our proposed framework utilizes a deep convolutional network to analyze each video frame half, detect areas with motion, and produce a complete frame through interpolation. This algorithm achieves significant speed enhancements and impressive results with minimal artifacts, outperforming traditional methods visually. It is particularly suited for real-time video playback.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron density distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to follow a universal pattern and was heavily dependent on the specific model used.

Precise and efficient river flow prediction is crucial for various applications including fishing spot detection, navigation, and flood risk assessment.
