The Itô-Wentzell theorem serves as a fundamental bridge between the Itô formula and the Chapman-Colson kernel, specifically providing the differentiability criteria for functions of the Itô integral with respect to rough paths. This paper formally generalizes the Itô-Wentzell theorem to a broader class of functions involving the rough path integral.

In the context of a scalable and private education process, learners random walk to neighboring neighbors to obtain training data from a large graph representing interpersonal connections. Following each training step, nodes evaluate the success of previous random walks and adjust their future walk distribution accordingly. A key innovation of this method is the incorporation of a feeding mechanism that prioritizes nodes with higher knowledge gain estimates. Through mathematical analysis and simulations, it is demonstrated that Federated Random Walk Learning yields comparable performance to centralized learning while significantly reducing communication and storing costs.

Three-dimensional wave turbulence is a theoretical concept that aims to describe the behavior of nonlinear waves through a collection of interacting waves. In a recent study, four-dimensional wave turbulence was simulated in a limited domain, and the results showed that the spectrum of energy follows a specific distribution (k^-3), which aligns with theoretical predictions. However, in a larger, infinite domain, the same approach yielded a spectrum of energy that did not match these predictions, until now. New simulations of one-dimensional deep water waves suggest that the spectrum of energy follows the predicted distribution in both finite and infinite domains. This finding is validated through comparisons with experimental data and is attributed to the influence of vortex filaments on the energy distribution.

This study examines how court-ordered mental health treatment for convicted offenders affects their future interactions with the criminal justice system.  We discover that participating in this treatment leads to a significant 3.3 percent decrease in the likelihood of being rearrested within two years.  This reduction holds true for both violent and nonviolent crimes.  Additionally, treated offenders show a 4.5 percent lower arrest rate for violent crimes and a 2.8 percent lower arrest rate for nonviolent crimes.  Our analysis accounts for potential biases and controls for various factors, including the severity of the initial offense, any existing probation or parole, and the offender's risk level.  We also investigate how the system responds to offenders showing improved behavior and find that being compliant with treatment requirements can lead to more favorable sentencing, such as shorter prison terms or the chance to serve community service instead of incarceration.  Our findings suggest that court-ordered treatment is an effective way to lower the recidivism rate among convicted individuals.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint. To accomplish this, a custom jFEX board has been designed for an ATCA base board, featuring a high-speed, low-latency design powered by two x86 CPUs and four programmable logic elements. This jFEX board has been successfully tested and shows promise in meeting its performance goals with a relatively simple design. Ultimately, 272 of these jFEX boards will be deployed across eight ATCA systems as part of the ATLAS trigger upgrade, expected to be completed by the end of 2018.

We introduce a novel approach called ANR, an articulable neural reconstruction method designed for creating highly realistic virtual human avatars. Based on extensive user input, ANR uses a range of facial and body features to generate a highly detailed, articulable 3D model. To compensate for potential errors due to limited or inaccurate input, ANR includes a robust feature normalization module, using data from a comprehensive dataset called CelebFM, comprising over 100,000 high-quality images with annotated feature maps. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in user-reported scores when using ANR-generated avatars compared to conventional methods, even with reduced and inaccurate input. Additionally, ANR showcases impressive results on challenging tasks like face animation and virtual try-on. Our code and dataset are openly available for download at https://github.com/younghwang ANR.

To gain a deeper understanding of chaotic systems' behavior at the microlevel, a novel approach using graph neural networks is proposed. By establishing a fundamental connection between GNNs and the Perron-Frobenius operator, a method is devised to extract explicit, physical insights from complex quantum dynamics through a multi-layer perception framework. The proposed approach streamlines the analysis of nonequilibrium systems by identifying critical time scales, providing instantaneous snapshots of microscopical coherence, and pinpointing key system components that drive macroscopic phenomena. Numerical simulations demonstrate the method's effectiveness with examples from both familiar systems, like the Dicke model, and more complex, harmonically coupled chains. The proposed technique is highly interpretable, offering a solution to critically examine the microscopical levels of physical systems.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by the unique parameter theta and a support that remains consistent across all values of theta. It's also assumed that the likelihood function meets certain criteria and that the maximum likelihood estimator, denoted \hat{\theta}, exists and is a function of a random sample of size n. It has been established that the mean of the distribution of \hat{\theta} is the known formula \frac{\pi(\theta_1)\hat{\theta}_1+...+\pi(\theta_n)\hat{\theta}_n}{\pi(\theta_1)+...+\pi(\theta_n)} and this result can be applied to a variety of problems, including the estimation of a horizon date for a cumulative sum process and the identification of the distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator when there are unknown mixtures.

Knowledge tracing has emerged as a significant area in recent education technology applications, primarily due to its potential to instantly identify a student's knowledge level. Many approaches have been proposed to improve the precision of knowledge tracing models, particularly those that leverage deep learning techniques. Despite the popularity of these methods, researchers face challenges in comparing their models due to the lack of standard evaluation tools. To address this shortfall, we present pyKT, a comprehensive Python library designed to evaluate knowledge tracing models. This library is versatile, allowing users to experiment with diverse dataset formats, metric options, and simulation settings. As a key feature, pyKT incorporates a command-line interface for convenient model evaluation, making it an invaluable resource for both beginner and seasoned researchers in the knowledge tracing community.

Given a polynomial map $\phi: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{P}^N$, we establish conditions under which a holomorphic elliptic operator has closed range when applied to global sections of a line bundle associated with $\phi$. This condition is met if $\phi$ maps the unit disk to a variety with a compact rational component. We also prove that if $\phi$ maps the unit disk to a non-compact irreducible variety, the image of any non-zero holomorphic function is dense in the associated projective variety.

We present Alethe, a new language designed to effortlessly integrate multiple SMT formats into a single, unified specification. This new language is capable of easily mapping to and from numerous existing SMT formats, including those employed by Lean, Isabelle, and HOL4. Additionally, Alethe's expressive power has been found to surpass that of several individual SMT formats in various areas. To illustrate the benefits of Alethe, we've developed a set of verified theorem provers using Isabelle and Lean, demonstrating both the simplicity and effectiveness of using Alethe with these tools.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronization becomes a significant bottleneck due to varying network latency. To tackle this issue, researchers have explored asynchronous aggregation methods in the past. Although these methods allow a longer time period for device updates, the current practice of clipping gradients is actually counterproductive, as it restricts the potential for learning. In this study, researchers first demonstrate that unconstrained gradients yield a better average than clipped gradients. They then propose an innovative buffered asynchronous aggregation approach that takes advantage of the diversity of updates by maintaining a history of contributions from each device. Theoretical and experimental results show that this approach achieves a higher accuracy than traditional clipping methods and even outperforms baseline asynchronous aggregation frameworks. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits superior performance in complex datasets and systems.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems are not yet widely used due to their substantial training costs. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome this issue, but it doesn't fully utilize the knowledge from a strong base system. Our research presents a novel approach to achieve high-performance cross-language and wide-phone-category ASR by building upon a basic system, without needing to train from scratch. This method involves two main steps. Firstly, a detailed phoneme representation is combined with a coarse representation to enhance the accuracy of the system. Secondly, the system is gradually refined from the language to the phoneme level. We conducted extensive experiments on RGL dataset and found that our method is effective in reducing training data required for target language and phoneme categories by up to 90%.

Twitch live streams represent real-time graph evolution, characterized by dynamic interactions between users. Evaluating node embedding techniques in this context is challenging due to limited information about the streams' historical interactions. This paper introduces TwitchPlayers, a dataset containing rich proximity preservation and structural role information for benchmarking next-generation node embedding methods. It comprises 1,000 anonymized player profiles extracted from 32 popular Twitch streams, along with 12 million past session snapshots. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TwitchPlayers by comparing the structural role-based node embeddings produced by three different methods: R-GCN, MUGEN, and TASTR. The results show that R-GCN and TASTR outperform MUGEN in preserving structural roles and proximity among players. Furthermore, we highlight the versatility of TwitchPlayers by evaluating how the dataset's performance is affected under different benchmarking settings and finding that it exhibits robust proximity preservation capabilities. Additionally, we explore the potential applications of TWitchPlayers in predicting player annotations and identifying influential players.

Our study proposes a qualitative detection method for a complex quantum state, $\rho^0(1450)$, within the $B\to \pi(K)KK$ decay process. By examining various two-body decay modes of these events, we strive to identify the signature of $\rho^0(1450)$ decaying into scalar resonances at around $1500$, as seen in the $B\to \pi KK$ and $B\to KKK$ decay channels. To accomplish this, the team employed a comprehensive set of theoretical and experimental approaches, including a thorough review of existing data, creation of large datasets with the use of Monte Carlo simulations, and an in-depth analysis of theoretical predictions for form factors. Furthermore, we outline the steps for a candidate's identification, such as comparing the observed data to theoretical predictions, eliminating background by means of variance and median-based cuts, and finally, verifying the detection through additional decay channels.

Recent observations suggest that dark energy's density Dim is declining over time, which contradicts the model's basic assumptions. As a result, alternative theories have been proposed, including one that suggests dark matter consists of Primordial Black Holes. We investigated the possibility of a universe with additional spatial dimensions and found that, according to the Swampland program, the size of these extra dimensions must be extremely small. However, this condition can be satisfied without conflict by a universe with more than three spatial dimensions. We proposed a model for such a universe, and using a semi-analytical method, we calculated the density of missing energy and primordial black holes. Our results show that this universe can meet the requirements of the Swampland program and that the density of primordial black holes can be as high as $10^{-6}$, which aligns with observational evidence. Additionally, in this universe, gravitational waves produced during the early universe's inflationary period may be detectable by future observatories. We also discuss the possibility of directly detecting Primordial Black Holes through their gravitational effects on the cosmic microwave background.

A key factor limiting the adoption of Series Elastic Actuators in high-precision applications is the significant error between the intended and actual control signals due to the nonlinear properties of the actuators. This study aims to mitigate this limitation by designing a novel force-regulating system utilizing a new mathematical model of the SEA and a sophisticated state-estimation algorithm, allowing for precise calculation of the actual force produced by the actuator. This capability enables the development of a robust force-regulating system using optimal control techniques, surpassing existing limitations of force regulation. The effectiveness of this system is demonstrated through practical testing in two scenarios: tracking a constant target force and responding to changing external forces. The results show that the proposed system can achieve very accurate force production with minimal error, outperforming conventional force-regulating systems in scenarios involving rapid force changes.

A liquid-layer raft undergoes a sudden expansion when moved over a thicker layer of the same fluid, due to a sudden decrease in tension. This phenomenon is observed in the case of a spherical raft. However, there is a specific viscosity ratio below which no gap forms, and this condition is determined by the balance of viscous forces and surface tension. A numerical analysis reveals that more complex shapes can exhibit multiple gap sizes, and this occurrence is explored theoretically by establishing a key equation that influences the formation of gaps. This developed theory is then put to use by analyzing a particular raft that is shaped like a cube, and the resulting numbers are validated through a comparison with existing experimental data.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multiparameter complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are represented in the fundamental category of the SU(Nc) group and are positioned at the point of high symmetry within the complex Lie group, known as the Weyl point. This complex structure is then characterized by multiple parameters, with each parameter representing a distinct mass value for the scalar fields. We've investigated the phase transitions of these gauge theories using multiple Monte Carlo methods, with a particular focus on identifying symmetry-breaking patterns within the lattice theories. These patterns are significant because they have the potential to influence the phase transitions of the corresponding continuum theories, especially those of electroweak symmetry. Slightly intricate charge patterns within these lattice theories require us to develop novel methods for predicting the features of the phase diagrams. By exploring these charge patterns and their effects on phase transitions, we've determined that certain SU(Nc) gauge theories with degenerate, multiparameter scalar fields may exhibit stable Higgs phases, even when faced with unstable charge dynamics that could lead to pole-dominance. These findings suggest the possibility of applying this knowledge to address the problem of polymerization in lattice SU(Nc) asymptotically free theories by constructing a suitable dual theory.

To optimize energy efficiency and performance for robots operating in energetic environments, learning optimal policies involves addressing high-dimensional input data and noisy reward signals. We address these challenges by using a Gaussian process TD algorithm, which minimizes policy errors while incorporating data in real-time. Our approach is tested on a marine testbed with a swimming robot, where it learns to follow a human leader despite being pursued by another robot. Results show our method's ability to adapt to changing situations, outperforming a comparison TD algorithm. Our analysis and the associated data are available online.

This paper introduces a novel classification of arrangeable networks called $k$-level networks, which are characterized by being connectable in $k$ layers. We have found that level networks are essentially a constant-depth variant of box-like networks that have multiple input nodes. Notably, this new classification subsumes the category of super-nodes, which are advanced connection patterns such as fusion operators, convolutional networks with alternating aggregation and combination layers, and BERT's self-attention modules. Interestingly, research has shown that arranging certain multi-layer networks is theoretically no more efficient than arranging single-layer networks, although implementing it may be more practicable. Nonetheless, there are certain arrangements of multi-layer networks that are more adaptable than their single-layer counterparts, and our work identifies specific examples of such arrangements. Additionally, we propose an unsolved but intriguing problem related to arranged multi-layer networks.

We investigate a relativistic, anisotropic stellar object in contact with an exterior dual-fluid metric tensor. The dual-fluid scenario involves two distinct fluids with interacting surface layers. By assuming an anisotropic energy-momentum tensor for the interior spacetime, we derive the conformal mapping technique to solve for metric potentials. This leads to a determinate anisotropic pressure distribution within the stellar object. Furthermore, we determine the adiabatic index by correlating pressure and density. The results are validated through consistency with known metrics, including the Tolman solution.

Using semi-analytical models, we explore how a spiral pattern develops in a galaxy like the Milky Way, with a high baryon mass content similar to that of the Milky Way, and located within a galaxy cluster like Coma. Our analysis employs a simplified approach to account for galaxy interactions and the gravitational influence of the galaxy cluster. By simulating a pair of galaxy disks with initial spiral patterns, and considering the impact of radial shocks and gas inflow, we replicate a galaxy like the Milky Way through a process of dynamic evolution. Observational features of the Milky Way, as reported in the second Gaia release, provide key constraints for our model's parameters. With these parameters established, we examine the galactic potential, stellar distribution, and bar formation in the model. Furthermore, our model predicts the presence of multiple spiral modes in the Milky Way, along with rotational velocity variations in the outer regions, which could be associated with a weak bar component.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that in a realistic cosmic framework, magnetic fields have a minor effect on galaxy mergers, despite previous predictions of a major influence. A comparison of simulations with and without magnetic fields shows that in a realistic cosmic framework, magnetic fields: slightly shorten galaxy interactions, raise gas sharing between galaxies, raise gas sharing between galaxies, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 50%, increase gas sharing in major galaxy collisions by up to 100%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 30%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 50%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 100%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 30%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 50%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 100%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 30%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 50%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 100%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 30%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up to 50%, raise gas sharing between galaxies by up

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%.

Most current methods for addressing grammatical errors focus on existing datasets' patterns, which can limit their effectiveness when confronted with new languages. This challenge becomes more complicated when considering that many developing countries speak over 2,000 languages, and it's impractical to develop extensive training datasets for each language. This study proposes a novel approach to correcting grammatical errors in low-resource languages by leveraging meta-learning, allowing for few-shot domain transfer. Our model utilizes a shared grammar model across multiple languages to extract general grammatical rules, which are then used to inform a shared GEC model via meta-learning. When introducing a new language, the model adapts to the new language through transfer learning, which involves fine-tuning the shared grammar model and generating GEC models for each sentence type through few-shot learning. Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of this approach on four low-resource languages in terms of GEC performance.

Rounding is an established technique for gathering sensitive information, especially when responding to questions about rare events. Researchers have shown that when asked about individual events, people round the true count to the nearest multiple of a fixed interval, providing an accurate estimate of those events that aren't infrequent. However, the standard approach falls short in capturing less precise information about individual items, particularly when the rounding interval is large. This paper explores rounding outcomes with a $[0,d]^2$ spectrum in mind, where $d$ represents the interval, and it's assumed that respondents use an ambiguous method of categorizing counts into two equal parts. The proposed model explains how people use two distinct methods of estimation: one for events that are common or obvious, and another for those that are less clear or fewer in number. The model also indicates that the way people estimate individual items depends on their perception of the surrounding range's center. The model is then put to the test using data from two separate rounding experiments, and the results show that people use different methods of estimation as expected, with the method varying based on the category of item in question. The proposed model addresses the long-standing challenge of Yagasaki's counterexample and offers a more comprehensive explanation of category-based rounding when responding to questions about less precise information.

Researchers investigated the magnetic characteristics of the one-parameter family, $x$, in the Gd$_{1-x}$In$_{x}$O$_3$ compounds using experimental and computational methods. The results show that reducing the indium content from $x=0.5$ to $x=0.25$ leads to a transition from a two-dimensional antiferromagnetic arrangement to a more complex three-dimensional arrangement centered on the honeycomb lattice. The change was confirmed by local magnetic structure analyzes using resonant X-ray scattering. Also, the investigation used the first-principles LDA+DTF calculation to explore the electronic and magnetic properties of the isolated honeycomb layer in GdInO$_3$. The findings are consistent with the experimental data and indicate that the indium content can be adjusted to realize two-dimensional and three-dimensional centered spin arrangements on the honeycomb lattice.

The problem of allocating essential goods to self-interested agents, where the number of agents exceeds the available items, is a fundamental challenge in economics, mathematics, and computer science. In this study, we examine a general, induced-bracing model that accommodates various well-known scenarios as specific cases. Our primary objective is to investigate whether this model's pure Nash equilibria exist and, if so, under what conditions the equilibrium can be achieved while ensuring a fair distribution. We establish a direct relationship between pure Nash equilibria and the optimal fare matrix and develop an efficient method for determining equilibrium prices through a fair matrix product. Furthermore, we introduce a non-manipulable, induction-based price-clearing mechanism and prove its effectiveness in generating pure Nash equilibria that satisfy fairness criteria. Additionally, we explore the computational complexities associated with solving fairness-related queries and establishing the relationship between our model and other prominent induction-based, price-making mechanisms.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation between source and target domains. Instead, we establish multiple source domains based on diverse sub-target classes and connect them to the main target class, allowing for a more flexible and generalizable connection between sources and target. This strategy is called 'beyond direct mapping' (BDM-UDA), and we prove it's feasible by developing a new multi-source domain adaptation approach, BDM-UDA. BDM-UDA is particularly useful for solving complex real-world problems with numerous categories and for adapting to new situations with limited source domain data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BDM-UDA through comprehensive experiments on multiple UDA benchmarks across images and text.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to constrain models of dark matter. They have created sensitivity curves for three types of dark matter models and taken into account two major sources of background, rock properties and actual detector capabilities. Additionally, they have determined the effectiveness of paleo-detectors in detecting dark matter when other detectors are saturated, producing distinct sensitivity curves. Furthermore, they have analyzed potential gains when using multiple paleo-detectors and considered various rock environments. Their findings indicate that paleo-detectors have a significant advantage over other detection methods, particularly in the sub-GeV mass range, and that their effectiveness could be greatly improved with more sensitive detection capabilities.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of a database remains confidential.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature significance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature significance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial sample analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The developed model has been made publicly available to foster further advancements in this field.

The task of identifying individuals across different cameras based on their appearances is known as visual re-identification (Re-ID). Although significant progress has been made on controlled datasets due to the use of advanced convolutional neural networks, there are still two major challenges awaiting resolution: achieving high efficiency for handling large numbers of identities and learning robust features from partially occluded and varied poses. This is because Re-ID is inherently difficult to train with labeled data at a large scale. To overcome these challenges, we propose an unsupervised individual re-identification framework based on contrastive learning, which is capable of efficiently learning robust visual features from partially occluded and varied pose images at a large scale. This framework is composed of two main components: a data preprocessing module that removes duplicates and generates pairs of identical and different individuals based on appearance, pose, and occlusion characteristics, thus creating a diverse and well-structured dataset. This leads to the formation of positive and negative pairs during training, with the former being identical individual pairs and the latter being different individual pairs. In order to prevent overfitting to minor variations and maintain visual uniqueness, we introduce a frequency-based soft parameterization for calculating contrastive loss, which is averaged over 24-hour video segments to incorporate temporal information. This leads to a superior unsupervised re-ID approach, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on five unsupervised and four semi-supervised datasets. Moreover, our approach demonstrates exceptional flexibility, achieving comparable performance to supervised methods with significantly reduced

This paper presents an original approach to a long-standing issue in financial modeling - dynamically identifying the threshold of a GARCH model. The new method, called BTGARCH, uses a unique combination of a studentized t-distribution and a hidden parameter to estimate the critical point of a GARCH model. A simulation experiment demonstrates that BTGARCH significantly outperforms the conventional GARCH model by accurately estimating the unknown threshold and reducing tail risk forecasting errors. Another finding shows that the new method's superiority over the conventional GARCH model is evident, especially in scenarios with skewness and asymmetry. BTGARCH is put to practice by applying it to a dataset of stock returns from the S&P500, revealing that the estimated threshold values align with theoretical concepts of financial modeling.

Recent discoveries of pulsar timing array signals at 112 MHz and 186 MHz indicate a common spectral index, likely around -2.4, which is unusual for pulsar signals. To better understand this uniqueness, we compared the sparsity of signals in various frequency bands using synthetic data, taking into consideration the unique characteristics of pulsar signals, such as wide bandwidth and non-linear relationships between spectral indices. Our research employed a novel approach using a Deconvolution Neural Network, which can handle sparse data and estimate model parameters with low residual errors. We tested this approach with various configurations and against established methods, discovering that it surpasses them in accuracy when dealing with data from wide bandwidth pulsar timing arrays.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough examination of the correlation structure of hadron momentum distributions is conducted via the study of parton correlation functions in the pion. Results indicate that the distribution of partons within the pion are well represented by the functions obtained from analytical models, specifically the Feynman and Boito models. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the parton correlation functions are generally well matched to lattice results obtained through the application of the Monte Carlo lattice approach.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models could be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects.

The concept of inequality of opportunity can be understood through the chance criterion, which holds that inequalities arising from chance are justifiable. However, measuring this concept poses a challenge. The chance criterion is closely linked to the idea of redistributive justice. We examine various approaches to understanding inequality of opportunity, including the use of the Atkinson index in relation to the probability distribution of outcomes and the impact of chance on individual positions in the distribution. We also investigate how inequality of opportunity relates to income redistribution. Our analysis indicates that inequality of opportunity is a key consideration in formulating policies aimed at reducing income inequality.

Removing a rank condition from a partial flag, we obtain a flag of rank r+1. The variety formed by these flags is known as a rank r partial flag variety, denoted as Fl_r. When r is 1, this variety simply equates to the Grassmannian, Gr_1. Investigating the quantum cohomology of these flag varieties, specifically for the rank r Toric variety, T_r, and comparing it to the quantum K-theory, yields the relationship 1/(qt_T)(\Omega^r_0) = t_{\tau_{\lnot\infty}}(qt_\tau(\Omega^r_\tau)), where \Omega^r_0 represents a specific Schubert class in Fl_r with leading coefficient 1, and the index \tau_{\lnot\infty} signifies the complement of the unique nilpotent point within the character lattice \tau. Furthermore, we establish a more intricate equation involving both quantum cohomology and quantum K-theory.

The complexity of modern machine learning pipelines often renders their data preparation phase in need of efficient debugging methods. Due to the large size of datasets typically used, a typical data point's contribution to the model's performance cannot be accurately determined through direct computation. Our approach calculates the significance of each data point based on a data-specific value representation, developed from the perspective of a machine learning model as an integrated whole. We develop a practical algorithm applicable to various machine learning algorithms and validate its performance through experiments on real-world datasets, finding it effectively identifies irrelevant data points. Furthermore, we observe that in some cases, refining a small subset of data leads to substantial performance improvements.

Our research involves analyzing pulsar candidates within 18 Galactic globular clusters using data from the MAVERIC survey at 3 GHz. By examining tier 1 candidates through very long baseline interferometry and radio continuum observations, we identified 21 confirmed pulsars and associated radio continations with 13 of these pulsars. By comparing timing and radio continuum data, we found that radio sources in globular clusters are largely powered by pulsars, with neutron stars accounting for at least 60% of radio sources. Additionally, we discovered that about 30% of neutron stars in these clusters exhibit radio emission. This ratio varies across clusters, however their average value remains constant, unaffected by the age or density of the cluster.

We introduce a novel hypergraph reconstruction problem, guided by a partially revealed hypergraph, where the objective is to determine a complete hypergraph representation based on limited information. This problem is tackled through the development of a new algorithm, taking into consideration three main challenges: unearthing the core of the partially revealed hypergraph, identifying the remaining unsupervised hyperedges, and ensuring the quality of the reconstructed hypergraph. Our approach involves an iterative process, first pinpointing the center of the partially revealed hypergraph using a similarity matrix obtained from binary representations of hyperedges, followed by the identification of remaining unsupervised hyperedges utilizing a hyperedge prediction function. To handle potential errors in the reconstruction process, a post-processing step is employed to evaluate and refine the quality of the reconstructed hypergraph. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in comparing guided reconstruction algorithms to unguided counterparts and showcase the potential benefits of our method in real-world applications.

Our study offers an entropic characterization of directional emission patterns in microcavity lasers. To achieve this, we utilize relative entropy in both its classical and quantum forms, comparing the density functions of laser operations within microcavity models and fully coherent reference scenarios. Our analysis examines the relative entropy of various microcavity models, particularly focusing on deterministic models and scenarios with positional disorder. Additionally, we investigate the heat bath operator of microcavity models and explore the Kullback-Leibler divergence's connection to the second moment of the coherent area, finding it to be a crucial factor in determining the emission pattern's anisotropy.

We examine the influence of heat on photon statistics from normally oriented three-level atoms in an open system, subject to continuous pumping with multiple coherent light sources. A method is presented for analytically determining the output photon statistics, based on the properties of the algebraic matrix representation. Specifically, we derive the moments of the photon distribution by manipulating the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a associated matrix. Numerical simulations are used to investigate the impact of heat on photon statistics under various conditions, including different levels of thermalization, constant heat application, and varying intervals of time. A key finding from this research is the emergence of non-Gaussian behavior in the photon statistics in response to heat, which is characterized by a decrease in both third and fourth order moments in certain scenarios.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical learning systems, as it allows multiple agents to learn without
the need for extensive labeling in real-time. In offline learning, agents
train on a single batch of data, interacting with each other. However, the
standard method of offline learning for individual agents does not scale well
due to the tendency for models to overfit shared environments. Additionally,
as the number of interacting agents increases, the complexity of the interaction
explosively amplifies the size of the data required for reliable estimation.
As a result, learning from data that captures the complex interactions between
agents becomes increasingly difficult. To address this challenge, we introduce
a novel offline learning framework called Good Path Learning, along with a new
method called Good Path Variance Reduction (GPVR). This method is designed
to minimize the variance of a function that estimates the performance of future
unseen agent interactions. The approach is grounded in the principle that
the best way to predict the performance of similar paths is by learning from
the performance of comparable paths. We evaluate our method through extensive
experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms the
current state-of-the-art offline learning techniques by a significant margin
in multi-agent settings.

Radiation therapy, primarily using X-rays, is a standard treatment for various cancers, with MV imaging being a standard supervision method due to its ability to monitor both tissue density and the presence of radioactive material within patients. However, MV imaging's application is limited by low image quality and the need for longer exposure times, which often results in distorted images that require processing to correct depth (z-axis) information. Our research focuses on enhancing 2D MV images by correcting depth information using 3D references, either from the same radiation source or obtained through other imaging techniques. To achieve this, we developed a novel approach using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), with our model's framework consisting of two main components. Firstly, a CNN extracts key features from both the 2D MV image and 3D reference volume. Secondly, a fully connected layer utilizes the combined feature maps to correct the 2D image's depth information. Our experimental results show that the proposed method effectively enhances MV images by correcting depth information, even in the absence of external 3D references.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Although Einstein's proposal was meant to demonstrate the inadeiciency of quantum mechanics, its interpretation has evolved over time. In the context of Einstein's experiment, the instantaneous non-local phenomenon involves the immediate correlation of two particles' properties following their joint separation. However, this effect requires at least two macroscopically observable entities. In contrast, the instantaneous non-local phenomenon associated with the collapse of a single particle's wave function has never been directly observed. It has been incorrectly assumed that this phenomenon is unique to multi-particle systems. In this study, we illustrate that the instantaneous non-local phenomenon arising from a single particle's wave function collapse is actually a consequence of its entanglement. Under specific conditions, this leads to a genuine non-local effect, such as the instantaneous transfer of steering from one point to another. This discovery expands our understanding of single-particle entanglement, revealing its connection to a peculiar, universe-encompassing influence that surpasses classical non-locality.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and Information and Communication Technology into the Internet of Vehicles has been exploring to enhance road safety and efficiency. Nevertheless, the prevalence of malicious attacks and data quality issues in IoVs calls for a robust Machine Learning framework that can efficiently utilize decentralized data while protecting against malicious entities. In response, Federated Learning has shown promise, though it has limitations in terms of security and performance. To address these challenges, researchers have been investing in FL frameworks for IoVs, including Blockchain and Multi-Federated Learning approaches. This study conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-enabled FL frameworks for IoVs, examining the architecture, security design, data management, node selection, sample selection, and outcome utilization. Additionally, it explores the advantages, challenges, and open issues of these frameworks, as well as potential future directions for this increasingly popular topic.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.

In quantum computing, the ability to perform certain tasks varies depending on whether a operation is singular (only affects one qubit) or multi-qubit. Investigating the distinction between single-qubit and multi-qubit operations within a specific quantum code can provide valuable insights into the code's structure and stability. Focusing on the toric code, a popular topological quantum error-correction code, we examine the separate effects of single-qubit and multi-qubit operations on its stability. Using a modified version of the stabilizer tableau algorithm, we create a comprehensive comparison of the outcomes of these operations, highlighting both the successful and failed instances for different numbers of qubits. Furthermore, we identify specific multi-qubit interactions that can circumvent the restrictions imposed by single-qubit operations, revealing new avenues for improving quantum algorithms through entanglement.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to represent a broad range of user locations and facilitate efficient communication. By reducing the codebook creation process, this method minimizes the necessary measurements and communication with the base station. Simulations indicate that the GMM-based approach converges quickly and outperforms traditional methods, delivering a superior performance-balanced reduction in measurements and encoding complexity.

A type of genuine 3D crosscurrent that counteracts a force in an out-of-equilibrium state has been demonstrated on a Hofstadter model with a nonequilibrium component, relying on the interplay between two kinds of tunneling processes. This current, resistant to turbulent-like disturbances, can be understood through a hierarchical classification of geometric structures on the lattice. It also shows immunity to the effects of random perturbations in the lattice. A method of engineering nonequilibrium lattice structures has been explained that allows for the creation of surface currents with desirable properties, such as speed and spatial pattern, by controlling the intensity of a driving force. Applications for this current system, involving artificially constructed 3D lattice structures, are explored for their potential to improve data transmission in communication systems subject to decoherence.

As a highly rigid object moves through a dynamic environment, its resistance to deformation dictates the rate at which it exchanges momentum with the surrounding fluid.  This study investigates how this principle applies to an object with infinite rigidity (a point source) that is emitting a steady stream of dust in the plane perpendicular to its direction of travel.  By exploring this one-dimensional scenario, the research models a supermassive black hole's interaction with an accelerating dust cloud as the cloud is affected by the black hole's gravitational force.  A key factor influencing this interaction is the rate at which the dust loses energy as it moves along Bondi radii.  The study finds that a ratio exists between the rate of mass loss and the square of the Bondi radius, specifically $\dot{M}/\dot{M}_*\propto (r_{\rm Bondi}/r_g)^2$, where $r_g$ is the gravitational radius of the black hole.  This relationship holds constant at approximately $10^{-3}$, ultimately enabling the model to accurately predict the rate of energy release through the accretion disk using a simplified formula.

We examine the early universe using a set of simulations for the first stars, and we focus on nuclear star clusters as they formed. By applying a mechanical process, we generate spectral lines for multiple star species, and by using a computational tool that maps the universe, we identify the sources of gravitational waves. In nuclear star clusters, we find that binary black holes with masses above 5 times the mass of the sun are produced at a rate of 0.01 events per nuclear star cluster per billion years. Nuclear star clusters that formed early in the universe have the highest production rates of these binary black holes, and therefore, we can expect to see gravitational waves from them in a rate of 0.01 events per century with a sensitivity to distances of up to 5 million light years.

The Gamma-Ray Surge simulator is a portable and compact device designed for testing the Gamma-Ray Surge (GRS) payload of the China Seismogram Network's (CSN) Gao Fang (GaoFeng or GECAM satellites. This simulator is capable of producing a range of Gamma-Ray Bursts with varying characteristics, such as intensity, duration, and spectral shape, in order to test the performance of the GRS payload under different conditions. 

For the China Seismogram Network, it is crucial to differentiate seismic signals from external Gamma-Ray sources. Therefore, the simulator is designed to produce high-intensity Gamma-Ray Bursts with specific features that are similar to those observed in the cosmos. 

The prototype of the GR Surge simulator has been developed and is now being tested at the Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics, Taiwan. 

This paper presents the technical details of this portable simulator and reports on the results of performance evaluations conducted with the help of the GECAM flight payloads at the Taiwan Space Center. 

Furthermore, we discuss the challenges faced during the development of this device and the measures taken to overcome them. 

The Taiwan Space Center's test site is also described, including the custom-built indoor facility used to simulate the satellite's operational environment. 

Finally, we outline the key benefits provided by this simulator in the form of its portability, high level of electrical safety, and the ease with which it can be reconfigured to produce a wide range of Gamma-Ray bursts.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-like spaces, specifically on BMOA^*, where f in BMOA^* implies that f essentially maps the unit disk automorphisms onto BMOA with mean oscillation. We examine the maximal subspace of BMOA^* where a semigroup of composition operators under a analytic function ph is continuous. This occurs at the index of 1/2. Additionally, this article is an expansion of previous research on C^1-like spaces, providing further insights on the continuity of semigroups of composition operators on BMOA^*. We establish sufficient and necessary conditions for a semigroup of composition operators to be continuous on BMOA^*, based on the derivative of the underlying analytic function. This article also explores the relationship between BMOA^* and BMOA, as well as the composition operators on BMOA.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, growing evidence suggests that the rate of new knowledge generation is outpacing the rate of productivity, an issue we term the Productivity-Knowledge Disparity (P KD). In this study, we collapse the vast scope of scientific knowledge into a unified framework, allowing us to quantify the P KD in mathematics and physics. We show that the gap widens as the level of expertise increases, particularly among leading experts, and that it manifests differently across various fields, being more pronounced in physics than mathematics. To address this challenge, we provide a quantitative benchmark for the effectiveness of knowledge transmission, highlighting that the P KD is most significant for new breakthroughs, while also evident in the broad range of specialized knowledge. To tackle this issue, we recommend a suite of metrics that can track the P KD, identify areas where it is most pronounced, and assess the impact of various strategies in reducing it.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications.

Two-dimensional systems with strong inter-layer coupling, like hBN trilayers, exhibit unique phenomena resulting from their ternary topology. This unique feature enables the creation of robust, edge-based modes within these materials. A new form of waveguide quantum electrodynamics emerges when these edge modes are coupled to superconducting devices. Research indicates that this waveguide QED undergoes a transition from conventional to non-conventional behavior, characterized by the interplay between chiral zero-energy states and natural modes of the waveguide. This waveguide QED features distinct light scattering processes, involving the conversion of chiral edge modes into natural modes, as well as mode mixing that could lead to the generation of exotic, quasi-localized states. The unique properties of these edge modes make them susceptible to sensitive responses to the direction of light incidence, resulting in an unusual dependence of the system's dynamics on the waveguide's termination. This understanding paves the way for the development of novel applications for waveguide QED systems.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. To achieve this, we've developed a predictive control system that can anticipate the human driver's braking pattern and utilize their historical data to determine a safe following distance. By integrating this model into their onboard controller, the connected vehicle can optimize its own speed to minimize the risk of a collision with the human-driven vehicle. We tested our method's effectiveness using a simulation and found that it can effectively prevent rear-end collisions with only a limited following distance, compared to traditional methods.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks that mirror real-world human interactions, including navigating complex systems and resolving ambiguous situations. Current evaluation methods for text-based games, however, are hindered by their slow speed and limited scalability, as they are often designed with basic functionality and are typically tested on players who can complete tasks quickly. To accelerate the evaluation of text-based games, we present TextWorldExpress, a modified version of three widely used baselines, including TextWorld, FieldGame, and SuperGLUE, featuring simplified goals and allowing multiple agents to coexist. TextWorldExpress achieves a significant increase in simulation speed, reaching up to one million actions per second on a single CPU, without compromising the difficulty of controlling the games. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of TextWorldExpress in conducting comprehensive and efficient evaluation of virtual agents.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in sequence recognition tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video identification, which involves analyzing long and complex video data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints, researchers have been exploring tensor decompositions as a means to streamline the training process for these models. This study proposes a novel algorithm that coordinates the development of LSTM networks and the design of their corresponding hardware, with a focus on reducing energy consumption. The proposed LSTM system is then compared with existing implementations using a range of datasets, including HMDB51 and Kinetics, with the results showing it is possible to mitigate memory constraints, minimize latency, and significantly reduce energy expenditure by up to 87.1% while maintaining superior accuracy.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability. Our research aims to explore the efficacy of data augmentation in enhancing NLP models' performance with limited labeled data. By comparing various data augmentation techniques and combining them with labeled and unlabeled data constraints in various NLP tasks, we found that targeted back translation achieved the best results. When paired with a small amount of labeled data, targeted back translation significantly improved performance. Notably, incorporating both labeled and unlabeled data surpassing existing state-of-the-art models like BERT and ALBERT.

The entropy formula for black holes in General Relativity, developed by Bekenstein and Hawking, can be expressed as the sum of an area term and an inverse-proportional term to the surface gravity of the black hole. This formula has been successfully applied in the context of Anti-de Sitter Space, where a relationship between the BPS saturation of certain boundary operators and the gravitational force has been proposed. We examine whether this relationship holds for all operators in a given theory, regardless of their charge. By analyzing the spectrum of operators in a CFT$_d$ using the CFT$_{d+1}$ as a tool, we can investigate the behavior of the entropy formula in a more general context. Our analysis indicates that the Feibleson-Hawking Conjecture is equivalent to a statement about the convexity of a specific set defined by the BPS inequalities, which we are able to examine in detail for free field theories. We find that the conjecture is valid for all integer values of $d$ greater than one, but fails in the cases of $d=1$ and $d=3$. Additionally, we propose a method for determining whether the conjecture holds in non-integer values of $d$.

To efficiently describe complex atomic systems, researchers have been using model-space theories like the Configuration Interaction (CI) semi-abstractly. Direct quantum simulation of multi-state systems is crucial for realizing these models accurately. A novel approach has been proposed for simultaneously obtaining spectral and correlation properties of these systems by utilizing quantum fictitious Hamiltonians within the model space. This approach is based on time-dependent quantum Hamiltonian theory and is unaffected by the size of the model space. It has already shown impressive results with very small model spaces, achieving converged spectra and correlation properties identical to those obtained from highly sophisticated CI methods. In this work, researchers will present an in-depth analysis of the proposed method's advantages and challenges. They will also showcase the development of an efficient algorithm for dividing the quantum Hamiltonian into two parts, as well as discuss upcoming applications and potential breakthroughs in atomic physics.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary invariant, we establish a condition for having a specific dimension in relation to its associated graded ring. This condition is based on analyzing various local cohomology modules with respect to a certain parameter and establishing relationships between their dimensions. We then apply this condition to identify characteristics of local rings that are strongly F-regular in terms of their dimension and their behavior with respect to prime characteristics.

Public initiatives aim to enhance auxiliary service usage, yet providers' pricing strategies complicate this goal. To understand this issue, a new model incorporates horizontal Bertrand competition and price differentiation, revealing that a significant increase in the number of competitors drives prices below essential service costs, making it challenging for providers to cover expenses. This difficulty is mitigated when the number of competitors is limited, allowing for price differentiation. Based on this analysis, targeted policies that take into account the complex interactions between market participants can be effective in increasing auxiliary service adoption.

R.W.K. Odoni characterized prime integers in terms of the properties of a specific polynomial, and demonstrated that these characteristics are not present in the powers of that polynomial beyond the second power. This paper explores whether these characteristics are present in the nth power of the polynomial, where n is a positive integer greater than 2. To answer this question, the paper defines a new term, "n-safe", to describe elements that do not satisfy the prime characterization for n. With this definition, the paper proves that a prime integer is an n-safe integer, and provides evidence suggesting that the set of n-safes is a prime ideal in the ring of integers. The paper also investigates the properties of the set of n-safes, and establishes a connection between the set of n-safes and the ring of integers of a number field. Furthermore, the paper examines the characteristics of the set of n-safes in relation to the field discriminant and Galois action. The results provided in the paper can be viewed as a comparison of the properties of the set of n-safes to the properties of the set of primes, and this comparison is shown to hold for the field of rational numbers.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production at the LHC, a new approach is being explored using the matrix element method to directly eliminate proxy particles and improve signal region definitions. This method involves utilizing the full dataset available for certain final states, specifically HH decay into b-quark pairs and all possible combinations of charged leptons. Although initially considered less viable due to a lower signal-to-background ratio compared to other decay channels, this study demonstrates that HH detection is feasible in the $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ decay channel with a data set equivalent to 300 inverse femtobarns of collision energy at 13.6 teraelectronvolts. By comparing the results of Monte Carlo simulations with experimental data from the LHC, this study establishes optimal definitions for identifying Higgs boson pairs and distinguishes them from background events with a high level of confidence. Furthermore, this study investigates the effectiveness of several sophisticated techniques to enhance HH detection, including artificial neural networks, genetic algorithms, and topological phase space features.

We investigate the potential of future $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and $e^+e^-\to \gamma Z$ studies at an electron-positron collider to inform the understanding of scalar electroweak multiplets. Focusing on a minimal extension featuring three doublets with arbitrary, self-interactions, we analyze how precision in $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and $e^+e^-\to \gamma Z$ measurements at the Future $e^+e^-\to$ collider can clarify unknown coupling constants in this extended theory. In a comprehensive analysis, we consider various scenarios for extended scalar self-interactions and examine how well future data can determine key parameters with a 95% confidence level. Our findings reveal that for most self-interaction scenarios, precise determination of key parameters is achievable with just a few abilitities in excess of the Standard Model (SM) and that a significant range of extended scalar interactions can be explored with a relatively low-capability collider. Additionally, we find that the combination of $e^+e^-\to \gamma Z$ and $e^+e^-\to Zh$ studies offers a more robust understanding of the scalar multiplet than individual processes. Furthermore, we find that future $e^+e^-\to \gamma Z$ studies can also significantly improve the precision in determining the $ZZ$ self-coupling constant. In the context of the LHC Run 3 and

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a hexagonal shape, a geometric pattern that forms high up in the atmosphere of Saturn, and was observed to be changing as the vortex within it evolved.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under a specific nonlinearity in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with solutions behaving in an explosive manner as time approaches a specific critical point. We demonstrate that any solution with this explosive behavior must satisfy a particular radius condition in the space $H^1(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \Omega))$. Additionally, we show that for a specific class of obstacles, solutions can be found that meet the explosive criterion and are invariant under scaling, given a particular dimensionless parameter exceeding a certain minimum value. Furthermore, we establish the uniqueness of solutions in the space $H^1(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \Omega))$ for the focused NLS equation when a certain invariant scale is entirely contained within $\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \Omega$.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The manner in which surface characteristics influence the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films has not been well clarified previous to this study.  Our findings suggest that surface oxidation has a significant impact on this transition.  This is indicated by two key pieces of evidence presented here.  Firstly, the metal-insulator transition is located at distinct substrate temperatures, as determined by in-situ resistance measurements and atomic-scale characterizations of oxidized and clean stepped surfaces.  Secondly, the amount of oxide layering on the surface, as observed using atomic-force microscopy and low-energy electron diffraction, serves as a precise gauge of the metal-insulator state.  Based on the results of high-speed photoemission electron microscopy, an attempt is made to explain the influence of surface oxidation on electron localization and the metal-insulator transition.  It is proposed that surface oxidation creates distinct sizes of metallic domains, as observed in the early stages of film growth, which eventually merge to form larger domains as observed in the late stages.  This is consistent with Bragg glass theory, as discussed in the context of V$_2$O$_3$ layering.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise finite-size scaling of BESPC by directly examining the implecation of quantum double dark-soliton states at the level of the Bethe ansatz. Next, we examine the scaling of BESPC in numerical simulations of the microcanonical ensemble. The characteristics of quantum double dark-solitons are represented by a set of strict constraints that distinguish two distinct regimes of particle densities. We find that in quantum double dark-soliton states, a first-order phase transition occurs when density changes from being extremely low to moderately low. The results of our study are further validated by comparisons with existing theories.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearization functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearization is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superising method for a graded bundle.

This informal note aims to provide a concise overview of key concepts in the theory of orbital integrals and the adjustment of measures, drawing inspiration from the work of Langlands, Frenkel, Henniart, Knight, and Vigneras. However, our discussion will deviate from their specific mathematical frameworks.

The measurement of nuclear states following a $\gamma$-ray pulse is a key aspect of spectroscopic research but is frequently hampered by issues with saturation and the signal-to-noise ratio. A new method was tested that uses time-domain resonant x-ray scattering to monitor projected wave functions and, when combined with additional measurements, can recover saturated spectra using a nuclear stage retrieval algorithm. This approach was successfully demonstrated using the upgraded upgraded HiRf detector at the SLS, which offers higher sensitivity and faster data acquisition. The new method was evaluated using data from f-frated $^{144}Xe$ and it was shown that it can yield a significant improvement in spectrum resolution, from 175 MHz to as low as 12 MHz.

This paper examines the relationship between quantum error correcting codes and classical spin models in a fundamental way. We establish a new framework for analyzing the stability of these codes based on the thermal properties of corresponding classical models. This approach enables a clear understanding of how certain errors affect a quantum system and allows its application to various classical models. We specifically investigate five popular quantum error correcting codes and, using our framework, identify specific thresholds for error rates that can be tolerated with the assistance of multiple copies of the code. We also found that some quantum error correcting codes perform better when their components interact in a non-local way rather than being close to each other. Our results demonstrate that certain classical spin models exhibit a higher tolerance for errors than previously known and show that this is due to the system's ability to distribute the effects of imperfect operations. This insight leads to an identification of better classical counterparts for two out of the five quantum error correcting codes and could be used to guide the development of new, more tolerant quantum error correcting codes based on classical models that are already well understood.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in their honeycomb form. Oxygen functionalization brings about unique filtering effects on the orbits, breaks spatial symmetry, and produces the desired exotic quantum properties. A key characteristic of this system is its large-gap of around 0.36 eV, alongside isolated Dirac cones on the edges which indicate potential applications for room temperature spin-transport. Investigations of the spin Hall conductivity and berry curvatures show high conductivity when compared to other Xene materials. These properties can be quantified with the Z2 invariant and Chern number both being 1. A practical implementation of this is demonstrated in strain engineered hBN/TeO/hBN quantum wells that exhibit a significant non-trivial gap of 0.11 eV.
