This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to diagnose Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work focuses on eye movement detection to identify this subtle symptom. To achieve this, we developed a new metric called eye movement entropy and associated it with a synthetic feature to train a dataset-independent model. We tested our approach using a existing dataset and found it capable of differentiating between healthy individuals and those suffering from Bell's Palsy. Furthermore, we investigated the feasibility of using artificial intelligence in conjunction with physical observations of a person's eye movements for medical diagnosis.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that qudits, especially those with a degree of duality other than 2, exhibit significant enhancements in this tolerance. Furthermore, our research identifies two key thresholds in noise levels that strongly influence the accuracy of mass gap estimations. While qutrits show considerable noise resistance improvements over qubits, our study suggests that the simulation of mass gaps relies heavily on the stability of the used gate set rather than its non-entanglement properties.

Research indicates that positrons are produced through the interaction of lasers with materials, specifically when taking into account classical physics limitations. However, calculating the exact density and polarization of these positrons requires a quantum electrodynamics analysis. By applying this framework to positrons produced by lasers interacting with thin targets, researchers have found that the positrons can be both densely packed and polarized, a effect that may be utilized in the creation of dense, polarized positron beams.

A group of order m by n (where n represents the number of generators and m represents the diversity of those generators) is referred to as a wide n-polynomial for the given group G if its Cayley table can be represented as the entries of n polynomials, with each polynomial of degree one with respect to one of the n parameters, representing the action of G on itself via its action on the parameters. It has already been established that the symmetric group Sn has a wide n-polynomial of minimal degree that is determined by n divided by 2 with a remainder of either 0, 1, or 2. It can also be shown that the alternating group An has a wide n-polynomial of minimal degree that is equal to (n-1) divided by 2 with a remainder of either 0, 1, or 3. Building on previous research, it has now been proven that any finite non-abelian simple group has a wide n-polynomial of minimal degree that can be expressed as (n-1) divided by 2 with a remainder of either 0, 1, or 3.

This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensing unit with a built-in conversion circuit, utilizing a single $45\text{nm}$ CMOS process. The temperature detector features a minimal design with only six active components, providing a precise temperature reading based on a $0.6\text{V}$ to $1.8\text{V}$ supply voltage range. With a $0.024^\circ\text{C}$ resolution and a $1.4^\circ\text{C}$ error margin, this design is suitable for monitoring linear temperature variations.

Three-dimensional simulations of stellar convection have confirmed the presence of magnetic forces generated by the interaction between rotating convection rolls. To understand the stability of these forces, one approach is to perform a linear stability analysis on models of globally consoloidally flowing convection, isolated in a large sphere. Any initial perturbations are monitored as they evolve over a set of possible modes characterized by specific spatial patterns. Analyzing the full spectrum of these modes provides a comprehensive view of a system's stability. However, studying every possible mode can be computationally expensive. Instead, we focus on a limited set of modes that capture the system's dynamics along its most unstable pathways. These include the characteristic pinching and helical modes associated with magnetic forces. Our analysis reveals that in regimes resembling those of high-resolution simulations, the most unstable modes are indeed the pinching and helical modes linked to the magnetic forcing term. We also find that in regions where magnetic forces are present, the most unstable mode associated with them can be suppressed by increasing the shear layer or by introducing small-scale turbulence. These findings hold significant implications for modeling the internal dynamics of stars with convection.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve complex problems by translating them into a flow equation, which can be seen as a representation of a fluid dynamics equation, and then applying numerical fluid dynamics methods to obtain approximate solutions. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address the challenges posed by singularities and high-dimensional differential equations in the context of quantum field theories. Our approach involves modifying the FRG flow equation to generate a set of partial differential equations characterized by distinct scales, which are then solved using numerical fluid dynamics methods tailored to various dimensions. As a first application of this strategy, we examine the $O(N)$ model across different spatial dimensions, and our results show that this method yields precise agreement with established outcomes for $O(N)$ models in one-dimensional space and predicts novel phase structures in higher-dimensional spaces that are consistent with theoretical predictions. Due to its general accessibility, we include comprehensive derivative calculations in the appendix as a useful reference for future researchers.

We introduce the Pied Piper Quest, a series of musical challenges designed to test the creativity of AI models on the Meta Quest platform. By leveraging the unique capabilities of natural language processing and computer vision on this device, we evaluate the ability of models to compose novel music based on visual interpretations. The technical details of our implementation are outlined below.

The significant difference between the Pied Piper Quest and previous musical generation techniques lies in the integrated use of multiple AI models working in tandem. We combine a neural processor capable of understanding music notation, along with a neural language model that both interprets the notation and produces new music. This combined approach allows the model to engage in self-reflection, as if it were a human musician, and produces unique results with ease.

We establish a local concept of geometric frameworks on Lie groupoids and differential stacks, incorporating a natural extension of the Bianchi-Minkowski metric. This is achieved by formulating a local 'complete' framework in the context of smooth maps, and subsequently defining a global 'complete' framework as the quotient by the action of a Lie groupoid. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these structures and the broader category of polynomial correspndences.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass-to-flux ratios, indicating a relation between gravitational force and mass, which may contribute to the formation of massive stars.  Further analysis of the most massive cores in the survey reveals a correlation between mass-to-flux ratios and the presence of magnetic field alignment in their surrounding environments.  A connection between the expansion of molecular gas and outflows is also identified, which is seen as a critical step for massive star formation.  Therefore, the findings of this research propose a new pathway for massive star formation, influenced by the expansion of core molecular gas.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of classical Godel logics with modal operators, involving modalities that reflect factual information within a framework of Inverse Semantics. This study explores the underlying algebraic and relational structures for these logics, building on earlier research by Arianna Gambini, covering several of these Godel modal logics, including those based on monodic Godel deductive systems, along with some of their extensions like modal classical propositional multiplicity and axonal Godel logics.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One essential step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various LiDAR 3D classification techniques using machine learning methods. Although these approaches have been explored in 2D image analysis, our study represents one of the first comprehensive examinations of their use in LiDAR applications. We invite fellow scientists to share their own findings and contribute to the discussion of future directions for this field.

The classic work by Matheron (1978) laid the foundations for the theory of stochastic partial differential equations through the concept of random fields, and his formula providing the mean response function has been widely applied. However, the availability of high-performance computational tools is now making it feasible to tackle random field-based simulations in complex geometries. This, in turn, creates a need to expand the Matheron approach to cover more sophisticated types of partial differential equations. Such an expansion can be achieved by modifying the method of vectorization, thereby enabling the simultaneous computation of multiple realizations at once. This, in effect, transforms the method into an efficient tool for modeling random fields. Building on the principles of the Matheron approach, M. R. Samavaki proposes a novel method for stochastic simulations through the use of the Laplace operator in a simplified form. This proposed method can be applied to a wide range of simulations, including flow problems, and has been successfully tested against established methods of simulation.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the neutrino-UHECR spatial associations.

Researchers studied the interaction between different liquid textures and a moving air-solid interface in foams, observing varying levels of friction. Through experiments and simulations, they found that the air-solid interface skims off more solid particles from some textures than others, depending on the size and distribution of the particles. This difference in particle removal is attributed to how easily particles are dislodged from the surface by flowing liquid. It is predicted that this phenomenon could be used to select specific particle types by moving the foam at an optimal speed.

This study compares the effectiveness of several deep learning algorithms in identifying outliers among dermatological cancer images, with the ultimate goal of improving skin cancer diagnosis accuracy. The evaluation was conducted on the established ISIC dataset, with the results showing that a combination of outlier detection using deep learning and entropy led to a notable increase in accuracy rates. The research findings indicate that feeding outlier information to the deep learning model enables it to recognize certain unusual patterns in the data, thereby enhancing its overall performance.

The influence of rotation on the evolution of a variety of patterns in a
slowly rotating Hele-Shaw cell filled with a less viscous fluid has been
observed and recorded for different hole configurations. By altering the
density and surface tension of the less viscous fluid, new patterns emerge
as expected, but unexpectedly, some patterns persist even when changes in
surface tension and density are accounted for. A key observation here is
that these persisting patterns exhibit flexibility when the strength of
rotation is varied. The occurrence of these patterns is linked to the
presence of a critical edge at the rim of the hole, where the strain rate
becomes infinite. The way the less viscous fluid accumulates in the corner of
the hole determines whether the pattern develops into an T-shaped or L-shaped
symmetry.

Building on previous work, a novel method has been developed which addresses the challenge of microstate nonequivalence in phase space. Initially, the method was tested on a simple expanding system, demonstrating that it overcomes the obstacle of microstate nonequivalence. However, the method failed to achieve nonequilibrium steady-state conditions in the long-term for the expanding system. Further investigation into the method was conducted using a freely expanding expansion where Hamiltonian trajectories were used, and a detailed analysis of the results was performed.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCN) is also reported, revealing they are around 30 times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. The ethynyl substitutions at positions 1 and 2 of the cyclopentadiene ring are distinguished through a combination of their radio frequency spectra and molecular structure, with scientists believing that the ethynyl group is more likely to attach to the more positively charged carbon atoms of the ring. The relative abundances of the CCH and CN variants of the cyclopentadiene ring are found to be similar, with the CCH form being more abundant by about 1.5 times. The detection of these ethynyl substitutions in the TMC-1 direction allows scientists to investigate their formation based on the reactions of neutral carbon atoms with cyclopentadiene, as well as through the addition of neutral acetylene to cyclopentadiene, finding that the latter pathway is more abundant by about 2 times in the case of

In neural machine translation, attention mechanisms facilitate selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target sentence words. However, research reveals that target word dependencies can cause lossy translation, with aspects of the source sentence being overlooked due to limited target word prediction. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a look-ahead focus to augment traditional attention by considering future target words as pseudo-source input. This allows the model to incorporate additional source sentence aspects, thereby improving translation quality. Experimentation with standard attention models on NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German datasets demonstrates the benefits of our look-ahead focus, with improvements of 1.0 and 0.6 BLEU points respectively.

The significant discrepancy between large-scale applications and lightweight devices sparked the development of grid computing to enable seamless interaction. Researchers sought to create a next-generation web services framework that could bridge this disparity by translating complex applications for low-capability devices. This goal prompted a major overhaul of the grid computing architecture, focusing on a transformational approach that utilized device description languages and descriptive abstraction to reengineer applications suitable for those devices. This new architecture was successfully applied to a pioneering project developing adaptive multimedia presentations for various devices. Furthermore, our proposed approach was found to align with emerging trends in mobile and ubiquitous computing, paving the way for future collaboration between the grid and wireless communities.

A unified dark matter-model is presented which incorporates a dissipative component to explain the present-day observed features of the universe. The model comprises two parts: a first law of thermodynamics application and an equation of state that considers both bulk and radiation pressures. By relating the bulk pressure to the entropy change, the model's properties are determined and its parameters are derived from first principles. Consequently, the model yields an adiabatic index close to $\frac{1}{2}$ and a constant temperature condition. Furthermore, the model involves a dissipative dark matter component which affects the universe's evolution. The model's dynamics simulate the hadronic process hypothesis's prediction of neutron-proton conversions, but with an increased rate. Additionally, the model exhibits a transition from a matter-dominated era to a dark energy-dominated era. Nevertheless, it is shown that the model is inconsistent with the given parameters fulfilling the requirements of a valid cosmological model.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and how individual differences affect this process.  This study also presents an innovative method for measuring curiosity in real-time, using a combination of self-reporting, video analysis, and functional magnetic resonance imaging.  The results of our study with 60 middle-school students support the feasibility of real-time curiosity assessment and provide initial evidence for the theoretical model's validity.  Our study's findings highlight the importance of engaging in curious behaviors, being open to learning from others, and valuing peer opinions in promoting curiosity.  Our study's results demonstrate that higher levels of intrinsically motivated learning, together with better social skills and higher cognitive abilities, are also correlated with increased curiosity.  Our study's findings suggest that curiosity can be predicted based on certain characteristics, such as intrinsic motivation with regard to learning, social skills, and cognitive abilities.  Our study's results also reveal the benefits of stimulating curiosity

This research introduces a novel Gaussian process model based on the Mat\'ern formula, specifically for predicting unknown node values within a pre-defined graph, utilizing a set of specified edge connections. By extending the Mat\'ern family through exponential kernel variations, the model is made applicable to non-Euclidean graph types. A specific focusing on Gaussian fields defined by graph triangulation is also explored. To determine model hyperparameters, an adaptive sampling method is proposed. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulated and real-world data applications.

Urbanized areas typically contain many unknown road details within their perimeters. We propose a method to locally optimize the detection of these roads using a wide range of ridesourcing vehicles equipped with GPS devices. The proposed algorithm can be applied to various optimization objectives, including minimizing detection time, reducing energy consumption, and minimizing the number of road segments to detect. We evaluate the performance of this approach through numerical experiments and real-world implementations. The outcomes show that our method yields better results compared to existing solutions. The code for this paper is available online.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) as a comprehensive framework that encompasses singular spectrum analysis (SSA), multivariate SSA (MSSA), and functional SSA (FSSA) for multivariate functional time series data. MESSA is particularly effective in extracting common patterns by applying the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) technique over different dimensional domains. Therefore, we provide a mathematical expression for MFSSA and discuss its asymptotic properties. Furthermore, we conduct a simulation study to examine the performance of MFSSA under various configurations. Additionally, we apply the MFSSA framework to real-world datasets, including financial time series and functional magnetic resonance imaging data. The results demonstrate the benefits of using MFSSA, and the software package RCMESSA is available for user implementation.

Deep learning-based automated emergency systems have shown remarkable performance in detecting medical emergencies, being particularly effective at pinpointing cardiac arrests from audio recordings of in-progress calls. However, despite their accuracy, concerns remain about their reliability and potential drawbacks, given their training on sensitive human life data. A closer examination of these models reveals both overfitting and overreactiveness, as evidenced by their tendency to make precise predictions on similar call recordings and their excessive confidence in certain situations. This issue is linked to their complex architecture and the implicit assumptions made during data preprocessing. Researchers have previously addressed overfitting through regularization techniques and data augmentation, but these methods only partially mitigate the problem. Rethinking the fundamental design of these models is crucial, along with incorporating explicit feature extractors to reduce unnecessary information and alleviate their reliance on derivative-based scores. Two potential defenses against overfitting and overreactiveness are proposed, involving the use of low-rank factorization and the incorporation of adversarial examples into their training.

This study continues the investigation of the global 0-1 law for the local time of a random walk at a specific level, building on previous research by Y.A. Kulikov and A.M. Vershkin. The new aspect examined is the sublinear asymptotic of the local time's expectation as the level tends to zero.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and it operates in two modes: an DC glow mode and a helicon mode. This study focuses on the plasma characteristics of the source in helicon mode, which was previously unknown. To understand this mode's plasma properties, a computer model was used, and the results were verified through actual measurements while the source was in operation. It was found that in helicon mode, the plasma has similar characteristics to those in the DC glow mode, except for a lack of negative ion accumulation, which may affect the plasma's overall performance. Additionally, it was discovered that in helicon mode, the plasma only extends to about 0.12 meters inside the source, and there is a distinct cutoff at this point due to the source's magnetic field. To optimize the source for maximum plasma production, modifying the magnetic field to make it more gradual around this cutoff point may be beneficial.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While machine learning-based nucleus segmentation has shown promising results in recent years, there's still a major challenge to overcome - accurately differentiating nucleus centers from surrounding tissue. This paper presents a novel approach, W-Net, which tackles this issue by dividing the segmentation process into two distinct stages. Firstly, a region-proposal network is used to identify and outline potential nucleus regions through a binary segmentation process. Secondly, a nucleus-refinement network is applied within these boundaries to precisely pinpoint the nucleus center. This two-stage approach significantly enhances the robustness of nucleus segmentation when compared to a single-stage method. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy and efficiency with W-Net.

Let's consider a non-archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either the set of special orthogonal matrices with an odd determinant or the symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted by 2d+1 respectively. A recently proved conjecture by Bulteau and Malle can be specifically applied to show that the number of two-sided unital module embeddings from the group algebra of G to the matrix algebra with entries from F is determined by a specific factor of an extended L-function associated with G. This statement can be further generalized to show that the number of non-degenerate two-sided unital module embeddings from the group algebra of G to the matrix algebra with entries from F can be determined by a specific factor of an extended L-function associated with G. This determination holds true under various conditions, including when the characteristic of F does not divide the determinant of an arbitrary element within G.

A graph G is considered traceable if there exists a hamiltonian path that visits each vertex exactly once. A graph G is known as repeated line graphifiable (RLLG) if its line graph H is a repeated line graph. This paper explores the relationship between RLLG and hamiltonian properties in trees, as well as the concept of hamiltonian path index which indicates the minimum number of hamiltonian paths required to visit all vertices in a graph. We investigate the relationship between RLLG and traceable properties in trees, and provide a limit for the hamiltonian path index of RLLG graphs.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by complicating problem dynamics and masking essential information. This knowledge about environmental impacts is assumed to be encoded in the state distribution patterns. We have developed a new approach that leverages state-dependent transfer learning to decode this information and remove the impact of external factors from the reward and state model. This decoded information is used to create a revised reward function and state model, isolated from the influence of external factors. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in both simple and complex scenarios.

A blockchain-based smart contract is a complex program with inherent risks, making it essential to thoroughly validate their functionality before deployment. Refinement types offer a powerful means to predict and validate the behavior of contract programs, ensuring they meet predetermined safety standards. Inspired by the refinement type concept, our HELMHOLTZ project aims to provide an advanced validation tool for Tezos smart contracts, leveraging a type system that combines dependent and spicy refinement types. By developing a compiler and validator for HELMHOLTZ, we strive to elevate the safety and reliability of Tezos contracts through a robust validation framework, capable of predicting the behavioral outcomes of contracts and verifying their compatibility with the Tezos protocol.

Deep Neural Network structures, such as Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental concepts. This study aims to enhance the visibility of GCNN's underlying mechanics by comparing their operations to standard signal processing techniques, specifically matched filtering. By relating GCNN operations to their signal processing counterparts, the study increases the tractability of deriving sensitive information from these networks.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is modified to include a scalar field with an arbitrary self-interaction potential, represented as $V(\phi)$. This modification leads to the formation of solitons and rotating hairy black holes within a new metric structure. As the scalar field's value changes, the solitons and black holes exhibit distinct patterns. For instance, in a scenario where the potential $V(\phi)$ follows a quadratic form $V(\phi) = \frac{1}{4}(\phi^2-m^2)^2$, solitons and black holes with various mass values $m$ exist, with the condition that $m$ falls within a specific range. However, if the potential $V(\phi)$ is constable, only the unsymmetric solitons and black holes with $m=0$ can exist. Moreover, in a scenario where the potential $V(\phi)$ follows a form $V(\phi) = \frac{k}{4}\phi^4$, solitons and black holes with any mass value $m$ can exist. As the scalar field's value changes, the solitons and black holes exhibit distinct patterns, with the temperature, entropy, and electric potential depending on the mass value $m$. Additionally, in a scenario where a non-Abelian gauge field is introduced, with a quadratic self-interaction potential and a Chern-Simons cross term, hairy black holes and solitons can

The proposed concept of non-reversible algebra simplifies to a well-known theoretical concept when applied to physical systems. Specifically, it relates to polynomial algebras that are non-degenerate when the flow of time is reversed. A key characteristic of non-reversible algebras is the presence of branes within the context of string theory, allowing for the realization of non-reversible algebras as boundary symmetries. A brane configuration corresponding to a non-reversible algebra has been identified for the W-algebra specific example. Furthermore, the connection between branes and the anti-involutions of non-reversible algebras has been established, leading to a deeper understanding of branes through the reflection of non-reversible algebras' properties.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in different directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral estimation due to the limited coverage of the synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound transmitter, leading to a well-known issue. To tackle this limitation, researchers introduced the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique, using a SA transmitter with a shifted carrier frequency. The VSSA technique is examined and validated in this study by applying it to simulated data as well as real-world ultrasound measurements, with the findings indicating a substantial boost in lateral displacement estimation performance. Furthermore, the study investigates the effect of varying transmitter and receiver positions on the VSSA technique and demonstrates its applicability to quantitative ultrasound elastography.

We introduce a new specification language that combines elements from pseudocode and formal proof, allowing the expression of algorithms through a form of mathematical reasoning known as sequent calculus. This approach provides a natural connection between computational algorithms and mathematical proofs, offering a common framework for both. By leveraging the sequent calculus, our language can derive both the execution of algorithms and the validity of associated proofs, showcasing the equivalence of pseudocode and proof. A simple example demonstrating this concept is presented, in addition to a discussion on the relationships between our approach and other established methods. Furthermore, we explore all possible permutations of our language's components and examine the theorems that can be derived with each variation. Our results indicate that our proposed method yields a robust and effective means of capturing even the most fundamental theorems from core programming language theory.

The concept of Ramsey character was initially developed in relation to graph Ramsey theory. Over time, it has been expanded to other areas of mathematics, including the Boolean lattices. This paper focuses on examining the Ramsey character of Boolean lattices by applying a V-shape relation to four-element subsets. By using a combinatorial approach, the minimum number required to ensure a specific color in a V-shaped configuration within a Boolean lattice of n elements has been determined for certain sizes of n. Additionally, this paper investigates the Ramsey character of the 4-dimensional Boolean lattices and provides lower and upper bounds for their Ramsey numbers in a V-shaped configuration. It also establishes a relationship between the Ramsey characters of the 4-dimensional and 5-dimensional Boolean lattices.

In the context of Euclidean space, a $k$-centers clustering problem exists where we assign each point in $d$-dimensional space to the closest center among a chosen set of $k$ centers, and then aim to select the subset of $k$ centers that minimizes the maximum distance from any point to its assigned center. This problem has significant implications, given its relevance to various applications such as information dissemination, viral marketing, and robustness in network design. While previous work has focused on static and Euclidean scenarios, our research extends the concept to dynamic and linear scenarios, using a new algorithm that guarantees a suboptimal solution with a small factor and adapts to low-rank data. Moreover, we introduce a new randomized approach for solving the static $k$-centers problem in high-dimensional Euclidean space, offering an approximation ratio that improves upon existing methods and unique benefits such as robustness to outliers and performance guarantees in certain cases.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale stochastic chase-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into secondary regions and determining optimal policies for each individual area. This approach yields a grid-world solution and provides a usable framework for addressing more complex scenarios. We also examine how the performance of this hierarchical method compares to a random policy as the number of sub-regions increases. Our results indicate that the hierarchical approach leads to significantly improved outcomes, and we anticipate this improvement would extend to denser grid worlds. Furthermore, we discover that the performance of the hierarchical method is sensitive to the size and distribution of the sub-regions. We believe our research paves the way for exploring more sophisticated division strategies and evaluating the efficacy of hierarchical solutions in broader stochastic game contexts.

A likelihood function that is in cycles with respect to a group of parameters is analyzed in this paper, along with conditions under which it exhibits nontransitive behavior. Conditions for a cyclic likelihood to have exactly three equi-likely parameters are provided, along with further conditions that allow these parameters to form a cyclic relationship of mutual likelihood. We also establish that a nontransitive likelihood requires either binary or cyclic relationships between the parameters. Additionally, we examine the implications of our findings on the validity of likelihood ratios and testing procedures.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring regular-dose CT images from low-dose CT data without paired training. However, the use of two neural networks in the two-directional mapping processes is not only complex but also inefficient, primarily because of the memory requirements needed to support both encoder and decoder components. To address these issues, a new cycleGAN framework is proposed that simplifies the architecture while maintaining high restoration performance. The proposed framework is based on a single, adaptable switchable cycleGAN architecture that employs an adaptive module for both encoder and decoder functions. By using adaptive averaging of the identity mapping, the proposed framework is able to switch between two-directional mappings with minimal memory requirements. Furthermore, the use of cycle loss and reinforcement learning techniques is explored to evaluate the method's performance in a realistic scenario. Experimental results show that the proposed framework is not only highly efficient but also highly effective in restoring regular-dose CT images from low-dose CT data, matching the performance of the complex unsupervised cycleGAN methods.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven dialog understanding tasks on four datasets in China, surpassing current state-of-the-art models like Multiplex Match and Multi-View Reader through diverse evaluation metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and rank.

This research aims to examine the geometric characteristics of an ideal fluid spacetime that is governed by the Einstein field equations, coupled with a certain scalar field and heat flow. We first derive a key inequality using the Conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric, and then establish conditions for achieving a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton within this ideal fluid spacetime. Additionally, we identify the behavior of steady-state solutions and solitons within this context.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that a distorted halo structure endures from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, and that collective excitations can be both prolate and oblate shaped, sometimes decoupling from the intrinsic shape.

A common issue with optical flow estimation is addressed in this research by suggesting two major challenges in video super-resolution. It claims that current video super-resolution methods fall into two significant pitfalls: 1) over-smoothing caused by unnecessary propagation of low-frequency information, 2) alignment errors leading to distorted images. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes two novel techniques: a multi-scale feature alignment method and a refined single-frame propagation formula. The proposed methods are then integrated into an advanced video super-resolution network (BasicVSR++), which achieves superior performance compared to the original BasicVSR in video super-resolution. According to the experimental results, BasicVSR++ delivers impressive performance on video super-resolution, especially when tested with real-world videos. It demonstrates competitive performance in video super-resolution while serving as a fundamental component for more advanced video restoration techniques.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and make lateral bounce angles with incoming particles, vector boson production within these collisions can result in significant forward-moving components being overlooked in conventional approaches. This paper introduces an efficient new method, called the Vector Boson Approximation, to account for these neglected components, especially relevant for forward particle detection in future muon colliders. Monte Carlo simulations have shown that this approximation technique can provide accurate results for forward particle observations within a 90 degree range and at multiple energy levels. Furthermore, this method has been found to significantly reduce computational costs by approximately two orders of magnitude, making it a practical solution for incorporating real-time lattice QCD calculations into the simulation process.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

Twenty-five years ago, in 1998, the first Godelian phenomenon was identified - a binary operation on the integers that is one-to-one with respect to each individual integer, yet fails to maintain this property when considering all integers simultaneously. Since this discovery, various Godelian properties have been developed and their underlying causes studied. This article examines four influential logicians from the past, Kurt Godel, Alfred Tarski, Rudolf Carnap, and Joseph Rosser, and how their collective work contributed to understanding these pervasive patterns. Their legacy continues to shape current research in areas like computability theory, model theory, and recursion theory.

This paper formulates the three balls conjecture in terms of monogenic functions, which are key components in Clifford Analysis, and provides a preliminary investigation into the conjecture's applicability to functions whose real dimensions are greater than two. Certain conditions are established to ensure that a function, which is part of a specific class known as $H^0$, can be linked to the boundary of three separate balls within a larger ball. This analysis focuses on functions defined within $\mathbb R^n$ and utilizes techniques from Banach space interpolation to support its findings.

When working with large datasets that contain geographic coordinates, such as population statistics, it is often necessary to randomly sample units in a space in an sequential and spatially equitable manner. However, traditional techniques for achieving spatial equity may not hold when units are not independently identically distributed. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative method for sequential spatial sampling that ensures equality by utilizing nonlinear metrics and Bayesian processing. The proposed approach allows for the inclusion of additional relevant context during the sampling process. Furthermore, the proposed method can be applied to contexts where the target population has an unknown distribution. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated in a simulated scenario and in relation to real-world census data.

To facilitate versatile robotic grasping, having control over the camera and image interpretation is crucial. While significant progress has been made in both areas, research on adapting the camera in an eye-in-hand setup has been limited until now. A novel approach is presented that allows a camera mounted on a robotic gripper to be adjusted based on analyzed images. By combining a unique motor control system and deep learning technology, the approach enables real-time camera optimization that can be trained from just a single image. The proposed method is tested on an Albanese head dataset and demonstrates improved performance over traditional techniques.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single solution, but rather on estimating the underlying posterior distribution, which encapsulates all possible solutions. This paper presents a new approach using a regularized conditional Generative Adversial Network (CGAN) to generate samples from the posterior distribution, by incorporating a novel regularization technique that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the predicted posterior and the target distribution. The framework is called RCGAN and is designed to be flexible, as it can be paired with any regularizer that complements the limited training data, leading to improved results compared to traditional methods in MRI image enhancement and image denoisy cases.

This article examines the concept of locally invariant manifolds in the context of dynamical systems and confirms that in the Lipschitz category, a surface cannot be invariant without being a hyperbolic invariant manifold. This validation extends to the fractional order dynamical systems. Additionally, restrictions are imposed on a surface's location and structure within a specific dimension.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is characterized by extremely short transmission distances due to high signal attenuation, but our proposed multi-hop protocol overcomes this limitation. In our model, we optimize the process of beam training and device discovery to improve spectral efficiency and reduce complexity. A hierarchical architecture is suggested for resolving this issue, where a central controller in each cluster manages the process of beam training through coordination with edge devices that handle the actual discovery and metering of access links. To tackle this multi-agent optimization problem, we develop a method combining reinforcement learning and optimization techniques to achieve the best outcomes for all devices. Through simulations, our proposed solution shows a significant improvement in performance by reducing the number of training signals, cutting energy consumption in half, and tripling the system's spectral efficiency.

The interstellar medium is home to numerous scattering screens, most of which have remained undetected. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns. We discovered and characterized 27 previously unknown screens at high galactic latitudes, near the center of the galaxy, where screens are least understood. From our observations, we obtained insights into the distribution and density of screens in this region, including evidence of dense screens with large sizes and low density screens with small sizes. Furthermore, our research indicated that screens in this area have a wider range of angles as compared to the solar side of the galaxy. We also found that screens here have a larger variety of densities and scales than screens in the solar side of the galaxy. Additionally, our work suggests that screens in this area have a wider range of projected lengths as compared to the solar side of the galaxy.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic expansions of convolution layers. Secondly, a pitch-dependent network architecture is introduced with auxiliary features derived from spectrogram analysis. Three experiments validate the improved pitch control of QPNet in modeling periodic signal components for unseen frequency inputs without additional training parameters.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this platform, as well as the results
of experiments conducted with the system.

As exoplanets are discovered at an incredible rate, the focus is shifting from identifying new worlds to analyzing their atmospheric composition and searching for signs of life. Thousands of exoplanets suitable for study are waiting to be analyzed with the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope. To efficiently utilize this technological advancement, researchers developed a new tool, the PCDetect algorithm, to pinpoint biosignatures in exoplanet spectra. This tool is particularly effective at handling temperate gas-giant exoplanets, which have atmospheres resembling those of Jupiter and Saturn. The results show that even with a relatively low level of stellar radiation, these planets' atmospheres can retain their bio-molecular features for an estimated 10 billion years. Additionally, the proposed telescope's sensitivity should be able to detect these signatures in exoplanets' spectra with a high degree of confidence.

To differentiate the signature of a Majorana mode, we propose using tunneling spectroscopy with ohmic dissipation and resistive electrodes. Our method involves setting up a topological insulator device in the Majorana mode and then conducting tunneling experiments with two types of electrodes: one with a high-Karplus constant that causes a shift in the spectroscopic peak and another with a low-Karplus constant that produces a shift in the opposite direction. By comparing the results from both experiments, we can determine the impact of the Karplus constant on the spectroscopic peak and potentially identify the signature of a Majorana mode. Additionally, we examine how the choice of electrode material influences the selection of a Majorana mode and consider two hypothetical situations to illustrate this. Furthermore, we discuss the feasibility of implementing this proposal using superconducting devices and discuss the importance of controlling ohmic dissipation in tunneling experiments.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road defects, yet their practical application remains limited due to the difficulties associated with manual data labeling and reliable system validation. Our research presents a pioneering approach to an intelligent road assessment platform, called RoadAtlas, which leverages a semi-supervised, multi-sensor architecture called the Atlas Framework. This innovative system combines a set of cutting-edge detection algorithms, including a customized dataset named PAVeph, to efficiently detect and classify pavement cracks, potholes, and curb malpositions. Additionally, RoadAtlas incorporates a robust performance evaluation methodology, named the Atlas Score, to assess the system's accuracy and reliability. We have also demonstrated the effectiveness of our system by conducting numerous tests at the University of South Florida in Tampa, and the results show promising outcomes, indicating significant potential for RoadAtlas to revolutionize the way roads are maintained.

The concept of shadows has recently been introduced as a measure for assessing the visibility of edges in graph embeddings. This study expands the realm of shadows to encompass a broader range of spatial representations, known as bicategorical embeddings, which involve mapping graph vertices to the points of a surface and assigning edges to the surfaces' regions corresponding to their connections. By extrapolating the principles of classical visibility to these new spatial mappings, the concept of bicategorical shadows is formulated. A key contribution of this research is the development of shadow-computing algorithms for various surface types, including 2D polygons and spherical triangles. Furthermore, a shadow-scoring system is introduced, scoring the information content of a graph based on its shadow-casting embeddings, which is shown to be useful in analyzing the network's topological structure. This research is relevant to areas like information theory, topology, and computer graphics.

Our research aims to address the challenging problem of localizing noisy areas within images that contain various types of clutter. In contrast to the relatively straightforward task of identifying objects within an image, our approach focuses exclusively on detecting areas with anomalous visual characteristics. To achieve this, we've developed a 3D shape model of images, which enables us to train a classifier using negative data that is derived from extracting noisy regions from training sets. By applying this approach to the AID dataset, our results demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying noisy areas with minimal additional annotation requirements.

Current Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operate within a fixed undirected and unweighted framework, but real-world networks often exhibit directionality and non-uniform edge weights. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel class of neural networks called Lorentzian GNNs, characterized by their ability to effectively handle positive and non-zero edge weights within a directed graph setting. Lorentzian GNNs are underpinned by a unique differentiable matrix exponential formula that maintains directional edge weight properties during message passing. We leverage this capability to develop two distinct models: Directional Temporal GCN for temporal prediction tasks and Weighted Multi-Task Lorentzian GNN for multi-task learning. Experimental results across multiple datasets reveal significant enhancements in performance compared to existing GNN methods. Our work provides a crucial step in enhancing the practicality and scalability of GNNs for real-world applications.

This study seeks to contradict a well-known challenge in the field of structural acoustic optimization, which stipulates that certain acoustic modes cannot be minimized through material modification alone. To address this issue, a non-destructive material substitution inverse problem is formulated for a specific structure consisting of two parallel plates, where the objective is to determine the original material properties given the replaced material's properties and resulting acoustic mode values. Since the model is highly nonlinear, a novel approach is employed by approximating the solution using a successive linearizations scheme, and validating the results with a range of challenging test cases. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to the stated inverse problem, and numerical simulations are used to examine the effects of different initial guesses, tolerance levels, and regularization parameters on the solution.

A new method has been proposed to achieve large-scale cooling of a mechanical system by utilizing a quantum nonlinear element. This method involves two main steps. Firstly, an optical cavity is used in a process called optomechanical compression to couple an optical field with a mechanical system, resulting in the correlation of their states. Secondly, a quantum nonlinear component is incorporated into the cavity to transfer the compressed optical field to another mechanical system. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated by a hybrid model consisting of a quantum nonlinear shifter. The outcomes show that it is possible to achieve significant improvements in optomechanical compression by using this method.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to paths and entities within a framework that incorporates a 0-ary modality. By exploring both basic and nested versions of this expanded modalities, we evaluate their comparative complexity in terms of complexity classes.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When combining the linearized version of gravity with harmonic gauge, it results in both the de Donder gauge and the conformal gauge being satisfied. Therefore, Hefty Gravity, which incorporates both harmonic and conformal gauges, is equivalent to Einstein's general relativity when linearized.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of polarity, a new category of graphs called signed graphs has emerged that essentially combines regular graphs with the concept of minors. The relationships between polarity graphs and the four-dimensional hypercube have led to the discovery of a new boundary in the space of graphs that are signable, and specifically within this new boundary, the class of graphs that cannot be colored using a certain amount of their natural number homomorphisms have been found to be equivalent to a specific subset of the four-dimensional hypercube. Additionally, the researchers have also found that by applying a specific transformation to the four-dimensional hypercube, it is possible to obtain a new boundary that consists of expanded double covers of certain planar graphs, and further that certain members of the family of minimized analogs of these planar graphs have maximum symmetry and cannot be colored using a certain amount of their natural number homomorphisms.

In the Weyl-Wigner representation, phase space trajectories of classical systems are represented by Wigner functions, which can sometimes behave negatively or positively, in contrast to the requirement that classical trajectories must adhere to the rules of thermodynamics. It has recently been proven that at thermal equilibrium, these Wigner functions must adhere to the principles of thermodynamics. This paper explores the basis for this thermodynamic coherence and identifies specific conditions that ensure a Wigner function remains non-negative within an arbitrarily small deviation from a state of thermal equilibrium. It then examines an example from harmonic theory to visually illustrate these conditions.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been firmly established as a valid idea with numerous applications across physics fields. To build upon this foundation, this talk aims to offer some general thoughts on the topic's bright future. I'll begin by defining negative absolute temperature and its distinguishing features, before discussing the various methods used to achieve it. We'll then explore the different ways negative temperature manifests, including within energy spectra, probability distributions, and flux or current patterns. Following that, I'll discuss some theoretical scenarios that could give rise to negative temperature in models describing dynamical systems. Finally, I'll conclude with some reflections on the significance of negative temperature in physical systems.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises all sums of $a_i$ with weights from the set of integers {0, 1, 2,..., h-1}. In this study, we aim to determine an upper limit for $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, as well as finding the minimum value of $|k\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where A is a subset of the integers.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

A novel numerical strategy has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This strategy's key component is an innovative, dynamically adjusted finite element method that utilizes spatially optimized meshes, characterized by high resolution near the inhomogeneities and lower resolution further away. To solve the problem, this method cuts optimization time by significantly reducing the number of operations required, while still delivering highly accurate results when compared to a more traditional approach using highly refined meshes. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the new method was applied to several challenging scenarios, including problems with large frequency variations and multiple distant inhomogeneities.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of calcium-aluminum inclusions from two recent falls, Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), which yielded distinct results. While the Chelyabinsk inclusions displayed a wide range of ages, the Benenitra group revealed a younger age with low dispersion, both consistent with the expected accretion history of the inner solar system. The varying ages in Chelyabinsk are compatible with the plancteal hypothesis, which predicts inclusions to have formed before being incorporated into asteroids. Conversely, the younger age in Benenitra is more consistent with the hypothesis that many asteroid planetesimals in the inner solar system were incompletely cooled and had thin crusts, thereby preventing older inclusions from being preserved. This finding is in line with previous research from antarctic meteorites and contributes to a better understanding of the thermal history and accretion processes of solar system asteroids.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ lattices, reproducing known results for spinless systems and extending earlier findings for the spinless XXZ chain. The results are expressed in terms of quantum-algebra operators, represented through the F-basis, and are linked to the affine quantum-group symmetry U_q(\hat{s}\hat{l}_2) for the A_1_(1) series. This connection enables us to derive explicit formulas for form factors and scalar products. Furthermore, we identify a specific subset of eigenstates that exhibit pure quantum-algebra representation properties and are therefore invariant under the dual quantum-group symmetry. This invariance is reflected in the modified Yang-Baxter equation, related to the quantum-algebra representation. The results we present extend earlier findings for the XXZ chain and provide exact expressions for the spinless Heisenberg chain's form factors and scalar products. Similar approaches are also applicable to other solvable models based on the XXZ chain, such as the XYZ chain.

Language barriers pose significant challenges in global settings, and language translation seeks to overcome them. While vast progress has been made in translating texts, similar advances in translating spoken language have been hindered due to the availability of limited parallel data and the inherent difficulties in audio processing. A further complication arises from the fact that many modern translation systems are designed with neural neural translation architectures that learn to map input sequences to output sequences, but these systems typically aren't capable of generating audio outputs. This paper introduces a novel multi-task learning framework that enables the creation of translation models capable of converting spoken language into other languages. The model's ability to perform translations is demonstrated in a zero-shot voice translation task using a limited dataset of paired audio and speech data.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

Building on the concept of quantum immanents, this study finds an explicit formula for elements of the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux, in terms of Schur shifted symmetric functions. This connection establishes these elements as key components in a broader algebraic framework that includes Schur shifted symmetric functions, Chern classes of Schur functors, and representations of the symmetric group and its central extension, the braid group.

Within the context of the easiest scoto-seesaw model, we have previously established that new heavy neutrinos and a dark sector consisting of neutrinos can interact with each other through both high-scale and low-scale mediating forces. Here, we are going to extend this framework to accommodate dark matter within the standard model extension. By doing so, we introduce relevant dimensions in the dark sector and incorporate a dark parity symmetry to ensure the stability of dark energy. Consequently, we derive the conditions under which the ease of the scoto-seesaw model is maintained, and subsequently, we explore the phenomenological implications for a dark matter particle of mass similar to the top quark. Moreover, we examine the constraint on the model's parameters imposed by the requirement of a stable Higgs vacuum. Within this framework, we also identify the possible dark radiation multipliers that could be discovered at LHC, as well as those that could be examined with future colliders. Ultimately, we provide the predicted rates for four major dark matter production processes at LHC, and we find that the easiest scoto-seesaw model can potentially solve the smallness problem of the dark energy density.

We employ first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic structure of transition metal oxides in the $d^1$ configuration, utilizing 3d, 4d, and 5d orbitals. Our analysis focuses on the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ splitting, a fundamental phenomenon in these materials, and how it affects their transport properties. Using a model that incorporates the blended $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ states, we show that the ratio of their energies can be adjusted through lattice constants and external electric fields. These modifications significantly impact the density of states at the Fermi level, influencing the metal-to-insulator transition and spin, charge, and orbital coupling. By exploring these effects in 4d and 5d oxides, we find that the latter exhibit more pronounced $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ splitting, which can be minimized through compression or external fields. As a result, 5d oxides are more likely to display large volume anomalies, quasi-localizations, and self-doping, as seen in various phase transitions and materials. Our findings also imply that the driving force behind many exotic phenomena in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides can be understood by considering the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ splitting.

Quantum field theories, when combined with geometric transformations, exhibit intriguing properties under certain transformations, particularly those that modify a smooth variety slightly. Researchers have recently discovered relationships between their theories before and after such transformations. This study explores how these relationships are reflected in the geometric changes, focusing on changes that involve small modifications of a variety's structure. It reveals that the relationships between the theories depend on a detailed, subtle aspect of the variety's local geometry. Furthermore, it establishes that two varieties have related quantum properties if their structures are similar locally, in a specific sense that reflects the effects of the variety's symmetries. This finding comes from analyzing the effects of the geometric transformations on the theories' underlying mathematical frameworks. It reveals that these frameworks, when transferred between the varieties, become intertwined in a way that reflects the effects of the variety's symmetries, effectively making the relationship between the theories a reflection of the variety's local geometry.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in medical imaging is being explored which involves using a pre-trained encoder to link latent codes to specific disease codes and then utilizing these findings to guide an editor of synthetic images. Our research focuses on pulmonary opacities, a common yet serious lung condition that requires prompt medical attention. We utilized a dataset of chest X-rays along with corresponding disease codes to train a multi-task convolutional neural network that can detect pulmonary opacities and classify their severity. By leveraging a dataset of synthetic images related to pulmonary opacities, we developed a framework which enables the editing of real chest X-rays to indicate the presence and severity of pulmonary opacities. We demonstrated that this framework can effectively edit real images to accurately identify the presence and severity of pulmonary opacities in a validation study. Furthermore, it was observed that the edited images with which healthcare professionals interacted had lower error rates compared to standard clinical practice.

ViDaExpert is an intuitive data visualization and advanced analysis tool designed for complex vectorial data sets, allowing users to easily explore multidimensional data spaces using appealing 2D visualizations and sophisticated methods. It provides innovative tools for identifying clusters, determining data embeddings, and detecting anomalies within the data, all while providing detailed information about each data point, including its proximity to neighboring points, cluster assignments, and multi-dimensional coordinates. Furthermore, ViDaExpert offers interactive capabilities for manipulating samples, modifying model predictions, and adjusting visualization settings, all within an intuitive interface. The software is particularly suitable for in-depth data analysis in various research fields, including biology, medicine, and social network analysis.

This research paper proposes a novel approach for computing second-order integrals over planar regions under Newtonian influence. By leveraging the method's simplicity and speed, even when applied to complex domains, it has been discovered that using a high-order quasi Monte Carlo algorithm yields highly accurate results equivalent to O(N^(-4)). Furthermore, the proposed technique is tested in a variety of settings, including both smooth and irregular domains, and is found to be a highly efficient and reliable method for solving a wide range of scientific problems.
